entry.title: Model company for SAP cloud solutions for Architects: From Target Architecture to an Executable Base
entry.content:
Part 2 of a blog series on model company for SAP cloud solutions

Introduction

 

Every architect knows the moment: the target architecture is documented in capability maps, process models and solution designs, but the next question is how to turn that intent into decisions the implementation team can validate and deliver.

This is my second post in the model company for SAP cloud solutions series. The first post introduced the overall proposition and the move toward Fit-to-Standard. Here, the focus is on the decisions enterprise and solution architects need to make.

Model company provides a pre-configured, executable SAP S/4HANA reference baseline with available industry and line-of-business content. It does not define every customer’s target architecture. Instead, it gives architects a working reference against which to assess capability coverage, question assumptions and identify the design decisions that remain.

Figure 1: From architectural intent to an executable reference. Model company provides a baseline for validation, not a finished customer architecture.

The Architect’s Challenge: From Design to Executable Reality

 

Target architectures describe what an organization wants to achieve; implementation teams must determine how that intent can be realized in a configured solution. The handover between the two often exposes uncertainties: Is a process already supported by standard SAP functionality? Which assumptions need testing? What requires integration, configuration or an extension?

Model company helps bridge this gap by making relevant standard processes and industry content tangible. Architects can explore and demonstrate a working reference rather than relying exclusively on diagrams or descriptions. The reference does not remove the need for discovery or customer-specific validation; it makes those activities more focused.

This supports a change in mindset, from Fit-to-Gap (“how do we reproduce what we do today?”) to Fit-to-Standard (“can the standard support the intended outcome, and where is differentiation genuinely necessary?”). The question is not whether the standard is always sufficient, but how to make deviations evidence-based architectural decisions.

Figure 2: Changing the conversation: assess business outcomes against the standard before specifying deviations.

An Architect’s Workflow: A Retail Example

 

Consider an illustrative retail transformation. The target architecture calls for improved inventory visibility, a consistent order-fulfillment process and reliable financial integration. Rather than treating every existing customization as a requirement, the architecture team can use the relevant model company reference to structure its assessment.

  • Identify the capabilities: map the target business outcomes to the processes and application responsibilities that must support them.
  • Explore the baseline: examine available retail processes and associated artifacts in the model company system. Confirm which scope and release are available.
  • Validate assumptions: demonstrate representative flows with sample data; compare the standard with key business scenarios and record the functional or non-functional questions still open.
  • Make design choices: Distinguish standard coverage from required configuration, interfaces, data work, and genuinely differentiating extensions. For each proposed deviation, document its justification, expected business value, and implications for complexity, cost, and long-term maintainability.
  • Carry decisions into delivery: use relevant process models, scope artifacts and governance tools to connect decisions to implementation requirements, testing and change control.

The result is not an automatically generated target architecture. It is a better-evidenced design: the team knows what it has validated, where uncertainty remains and which decisions require architectural ownership.

 

How It Helps Enterprise Architects

 

Enterprise architects connect strategy, business capabilities and the target operating model with the application landscape.

Model company can help them:

  • Assess capability realization in a running reference and distinguish demonstrated scope from capabilities that still require further design.
  • Relate reference business architecture and process models to the actual standard processes delivered in the relevant industry or line of business.
  • Create a shared starting point for business stakeholders, enterprise architecture and delivery teams, reducing misunderstandings about what “standard” means.
  • Inform roadmap and scoping decisions by checking current content availability, release coverage and relevant prerequisites rather than assuming that every planned capability is already delivered.

How It Helps Solution Architects

 

Solution architects translate the target into process, data, application, integration and extension decisions. Against a pre-configured reference, they can:

  • Explore representative end-to-end processes instead of starting each discussion from an unconfigured system.
  • Inspect sample master and transactional data and identify interfaces or integration requirements; a visible integration point does not necessarily mean that a connected external system has been delivered.
  • Evaluate standard functionality first, then select suitable clean-core-aligned extensibility options based on the requirement and deployment environment.
  • Use process and delivery artifacts to support documented scope, requirements and testing decisions, with traceability governed through the chosen project toolchain.

Connecting Architecture to the Delivery Toolchain

 

SAP LeanIX supports enterprise architecture and application landscape decisions; SAP Signavio provides a comprehensive process intelligence and transformation suite for process-modeling and business transformation; and SAP Cloud ALM is a full lifecycle application management platform, covering implementation governance, operations monitoring, and continuous improvement.

For transformation initiatives, it delivers end-to-end project management, structured requirements handling, and test governance, making it the central control point for managing SAP solution deployments.

Model company contributes a working reference and associated artifacts that can be used alongside these tools.

The precise artifacts available depend on the selected model company scope and release. Process models, documentation, test assets and sample data can support design and Fit-to-Standard workshops, but architects should verify what is included and how it can be accessed or imported. Viewing process content and importing or synchronizing it into a customer workspace may have different licensing and authorization requirements.

Importantly, traceability is not automatic. Connecting process models, scope, requirements and test evidence requires tool configuration, appropriate entitlements, disciplined ownership and project governance. SAP Signavio, SAP Cloud ALM synchronization, for example, has defined setup and license prerequisites.

 

Where It Fits in SAP Activate

 

Model company brings its most immediate value to early validation and Fit-to-Standard work, particularly during Explore. Its reference content and artifacts may also inform later implementation phases.

The model company system remains a reference/sandbox environment: it is not the productive customer solution and should not be described as directly deploying into production.

  • Discover and Prepare: use the available baseline to illustrate potential scope, challenge target-state assumptions and prepare more focused architectural discussions.
  • Explore (Fit-to-Standard): run relevant scenarios against the standard, assess business fit, identify genuine deltas and agree which requirements need additional design.
  • Realize: use validated decisions and applicable reference artifacts to guide implementation; govern architecture conformance, interfaces, extensions and test coverage in the customer project.
  • Deploy: confirm that the implemented productive solution meets the approved architecture, security, integration and operational criteria. This is a customer-project responsibility, not a deployment of the model company sandbox.
  • Run: maintain architectural guardrails, assess changing needs against standard capabilities, and govern extensions and process evolution over time.

The continuous thread is controlled decision-making: from intended business capability, through process validation and design, to implementation evidence. The architecture team can establish traceability across that chain but must actively maintain it.

Figure 3: Model company in SAP Activate. Explore is the primary direct validation point; later phases benefit from the reference and decisions carried forward.

Keeping the Core Clean: Extensibility Governance

 

Clean core is an architectural discipline, not a property that eliminates governance. It aims to keep the SAP core close to standard, use appropriate extension mechanisms and released interfaces, and support maintainability and future upgrades. Model company, built on SAP Best Practices that bring standard Line of Business business processes and aligned with clean-core principles, gives architects a useful starting reference, not an unconditional guarantee of customer-specific compliance or upgrade safety.

  • Challenge proposed deviations: demonstrate what standard content already covers before agreeing to custom build; record business rationale and architectural consequences for justified gaps.
  • Choose the right extension pattern: consider approved key-user, developer/on-stack and side-by-side extensibility, including SAP BTP where appropriate. The right choice depends on requirements, release and deployment model; “side-by-side” is not the answer to every extension.
  • Govern integration explicitly: design interfaces around applicable released APIs and supported integration patterns, while validating external systems, security, performance and data responsibilities.
  • Keep decisions traceable: link requirements, architectural decisions, process changes and tests within the project’s governed toolchain, rather than assuming the reference environment does this automatically.

By reducing unnecessary custom code and providing a clean-core-aligned reference, model company simplifies architectural decision-making and lifecycle management, while enabling architects to focus their assessments on customer-specific requirements, integrations, and extensions.

 

What Architects Still Need to Validate

 

A reference baseline is most useful when its boundaries are clear.

Architects must still confirm:

  • Industry and country coverage
  • Business-process fit
  • The customer’s application and integration landscape
  • Data migration and ownership
  • Non-functional requirements
  • Security and regulatory obligations
  • Extension design
  • Licensing or technical prerequisites for connected tools.

The strongest use of model company is therefore not to declare the architecture complete. It is to expose and resolve architectural questions earlier, while keeping legitimate differentiation visible and controlled.

 

From Clean Core to Validated AI Capabilities

 

Clean-core principles, standardized processes, and governed data provide a strong foundation for sustainable AI adoption. Model company for SAP cloud solutions builds on this foundation, with Joule already activated and successfully tested in selected model company environments. In addition, AI use cases have been tested and validated and are ready for inclusion, progressively extending the portfolio’s ability to demonstrate AI-enabled business processes.

For architects, this creates an opportunity to move beyond conceptual AI discussions and explore how intelligent capabilities can be incorporated into business processes and solution architectures. These validated scenarios provide tangible reference points for assessing architectural dependencies, integration requirements, and the potential role of AI within a customer’s target landscape.

AI enablement is progressing across the model company portfolio, with capabilities and availability varying by industry and line of business. Their adoption within a customer environment remains subject to scenario availability, release compatibility, licensing and entitlements, technical prerequisites, and applicable AI consumption arrangements.

By combining a clean-core-aligned baseline with activated Joule capabilities and validated AI use cases, model company helps architects bridge the gap between AI strategy and practical enablement.

 

Conclusion: A Better Starting Point for Architectural Decisions

 

Model company changes the starting point, not the architect’s responsibility. Instead of working only from abstract models or a blank configuration, teams can examine a tangible, SAP-delivered baseline and use it to validate assumptions, challenge unnecessary complexity and make more informed Fit-to-Standard decisions.

Whether your role is enterprise architecture or solution architecture, the benefit is a clearer distinction between what the reference already demonstrates, what the customer genuinely needs and what must still be designed and governed.

Start with one critical capability from your target architecture. Explore the model company content available for the relevant industry, test the associated process assumptions and document where the standard fits or where further decisions are needed.

What is the harder challenge in your projects:

  • Validating standard coverage
  • Designing integrations
  • Governing extensions?

Share your experience in the comments.

For availability and request guidance, consult your model company industry/Line of Business dashboard or contact modelcompany@sap.com. For scope selection and applicable terms, refer to SAP Note 3631601 through your normal SAP support channel.

 

Continue the Series

 

If you missed Part 1, read Model company for SAP cloud solutions: Your Fast Track to Fit-to-Standard. Upcoming topics will explore the consultant, partner and content/toolchain perspectives.

entry.title: Stop Clicking, Start Scripting: Automate BTP Role Collection Mapping to IAS Groups via REST APIs
entry.content:
Introduction

Picture this: a customer is going live with a new SAP BTP landscape. Their IAS tenant already has user groups set up, their role collections are defined, and all that's left is connecting the two. Simple enough: in the BTP cockpit, navigate to Security → Trust Configuration → your IAS trust → Role Collection Mappings, and add one mapping at a time.

Now imagine doing that hundreds of times.

That was the reality for one of my customers. 130 role collections, each needing to be mapped to its corresponding IAS user group. At a conservative 3-4 minutes per mapping, finding the right collection, typing the group name exactly right, saving, repeat. You're looking at close to 8 hours of repetitive, error-prone cockpit work.

As a BTP consultant, I've seen this scenario play out more than once. And every time, the frustration is the same: the platform has everything you need, yet you're stuck doing something a machine should be doing for you.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service REST API to map BTP role collections to IAS user groups programmatically, saving hours of manual work, eliminating typo-induced errors, and giving you a reusable script you can run across every environment in your landscape.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place:

  • Subaccount Administrator role collection assigned to your user in the target BTP subaccount
  • A BTP subaccount with an IAS tenant configured as a custom identity provider
  • IAS user groups already created and populated with users
  • BTP CLI installed and configured
  • A REST client for testing: curl, Postman, or Bruno all work fine
  • Node.js (v18+) for the automation script (if you're creating a Node.js script like me)

 

Let's get scripting

Step 1 — Get API Credentials via the BTP CLI

To call the XSUAA REST API, you need a client credential pair. The cleanest way to get one is directly through the BTP CLI. No service instance or service key required.

btp login --sso
btp target --subaccount <SUBACCOUNT_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

Note:  This is the current recommended approach, replacing the deprecated apiaccess XSUAA service plan. If you come across older tutorials using "cf create-service xsuaa apiaccess" that approach still works but is being phased out.

The command returns a JSON object. Save these four values, you'll need all of them:

  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url (the token endpoint)
  • apiurl (the API base URL)

Step 2 — Get a Bearer Token

With the credentials in hand, request an OAuth token using the client credentials flow:

curl --request POST \
--url <url> \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data 'client_id=<clientid>' \
--data 'client_secret=<clientsecret>' \
--data 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
--data 'response_type=token'

Copy the access_token value from the response. You'll use it as a Bearer token in the next steps.

Step 3 — Check Existing Mappings (Optional but Recommended)

Before writing anything, it's worth checking what mappings already exist for your IAS identity provider. This gives you a baseline and avoids surprises:

curl --request GET \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>'

Where to find the IAS Origin Key: In your BTP subaccount, go to Security → Trust Configuration and click on your IAS trust entry. The Origin Key is shown in the detail panel. It typically looks like <something>.accounts.ondemand.com.

Step 4 — Create a Single Mapping

Now for the actual mapping call. Let's do one manually first to confirm everything works before running a bulk script:

curl --request POST \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>' \
--header 'content-type: application/json' \
--data '{
"attributeName": "Groups",
"attributeValue": "<IAS_Group_Name>",
"operator": "equals",
"roleCollectionName": "<BTP_Role_Collection_Name>"
}'

A few things to pay attention to:

  • attributeName must be exactly "Groups" with capital G, case-sensitive. This is the single most common mistake, and it fails without a helpful error message, so double-check this first.
  • attributeValue is the IAS group name, not the group ID.
  • roleCollectionName must match the role collection name exactly as it appears in the BTP cockpit.

A successful call returns HTTP 201 with the created mapping. To verify: go to BTP Cockpit → Security → Role Collections → open your role collection → User Groups tab. Your IAS group should now appear there.

Step 5 — Scale It Up: Automate with a Node.js Script

One mapping confirmed, now let's do all 130. The script below reads a list of mappings from a JSON file, fetches a token, and loops through each entry.

Project structure:

  • mappings.json – your list of group → role collection pairs
  • map-roles.mjs – the script
  • .env – credentials (never commit or publish this!)

.env

TOKEN_URL=https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
API_URL=https://api.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com
IAS_ORIGIN_KEY=<your-ias-origin-key>

mappings.json

[
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_ADMINS",
        "roleCollection": "Subaccount Administrator"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_DEVELOPERS",
        "roleCollection": "Extension Developer"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "CPI_OPERATORS",
        "roleCollection": "PI Business Expert"
    }
]

map-roles.mjs

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import 'dotenv/config';

const { TOKEN_URL, CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, API_URL, IAS_ORIGIN_KEY } = process.env;

async function getToken() {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
        grant_type: 'client_credentials',
        response_type: 'token',
        client_id: CLIENT_ID,
        client_secret: CLIENT_SECRET
    });
    const res = await fetch(TOKEN_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
        body: params
    });
    const { access_token } = await res.json();
    return access_token;
}

async function mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection) {
    const url = `${API_URL}/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/${IAS_ORIGIN_KEY}/attributes`;
    const res = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
            Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            Accept: 'application/json'
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            attributeName: 'Groups',
            attributeValue: iasGroup,
            operator: 'equals',
            roleCollectionName: roleCollection
        })
    });

    if (res.status === 409) {
        console.log(`Already mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (res.status === 404) {
        console.error(`Not found (check name): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (!res.ok) {
        console.error(`Failed (${res.status}): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    console.log(`Mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
}

const mappings = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./mappings.json', 'utf-8'));
const token = await getToken();

for (const { iasGroup, roleCollection } of mappings) {
    await mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection);
}

Install the one dependency and run:

npm install dotenv
node map-roles.mjs

You'll see a clear log for every mapping: success, already exists, or failure with the exact entry so you can investigate.

Bonus: Multi-Environment Reuse

Once your mappings.json is ready, deploying to multiple environments is trivial. Re-target the BTP CLI and generate a fresh set of credentials for each subaccount:

btp target --subaccount <DEV_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# next subaccount 
btp target --subaccount <QA_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# and so on ...

What was an 8-hour cockpit exercise becomes a 2-minute operation per environment. Repeatable, consistent, and auditable.

 

Conclusion

The SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service API is one of those tools that, once you know it's there, you'll reach for regularly. The manual cockpit approach is fine for a handful of mappings, but as soon as you're dealing with real-world project complexity with dozens of role collections, multiple environments, repeated deployments, it simply doesn't scale.

The setup described in this post takes maybe 30 minutes the first time: prepare your mappings.json, configure the .env, run one test call to validate. After that, it's just a matter of running the script. For the customer that inspired this post, what would have been a full day of clicking was done before lunch.

If you give this a try, I'd love to hear how it works for you especially if you adapt the script or extend it to cover other security artifacts. Drop a comment below or reach out directly.

entry.title: Understanding the changes to Rehires in H2 2026 Onboarding release.
entry.content:
In the H2 release for Onboarding there are some significant changes to how the rehire process works.  There is a very detailed blog here.  However, we have tried to distil this even further for users to understand easily.

Before we start it is interesting to confirm how rehires work in Employee Central. 

In Employee Central if you have a Contingent Worker (CW) whose end date has passed, you can’t rehire onto that record as an employee or a CW.  You need a ‘Rehire on a New Employment’. 

You can extend a contingent worker if the end date has not passed but once it is passed you can’t change the end date you need to do a rehire.

Scenario A – Rehiring an inactive contingent worker as an employee

Let’s assume we you have a contingent worker whose work order end date has passed and they are inactive.  If they were returning via onboarding as an employee, the system (prior to this release) would allow you to ‘Rehire on the Old Employment’ onto the inactive CW record.  This action would throw errors in Employee Central as it is not allowed.  As a result, in this release you can no longer do this.  The system will force you to rehire on a new employment as this is how it works in Employee Central.

 

Scenario B – Rehiring an inactive contingent worker as an employee

Let’s assume we you have a contingent worker whose work order end date has passed and they have a separate inactive employee record i.e. they have two inactive records.  If they were returning via onboarding as an employee, the system will allow you to rehire on the old employee record (subject to RBP) on the employee record or Rehire on a New Employment. It won’t allow you to rehire on the old employment on the CW worker record as described in Scenario A.

 

Scenario C – Rehiring an active contingent worker as an employee with a future date termination

If you had a contingent worker whose work order end date is in the future.  You can now rehire as an employee with a new employment after the future dated termination.

 Additional Comments

  1. If you have an employee who has a future date termination and you want to rehire them via onboarding, the system only supports Rehire on New Employment and not Rehire on Old Employment.  This has not changed in this release. 
  2.  
  3. When you perform the rehire checks.  In the release product talks about adding in a ‘surface layers’, these are effectively new pop up screens to help you process the rehire.  For rehire on old employment you can add in the correct event reason without having to complete the whole process.

If there are any data errors when you rehire you will be redirected to adjust the data errors, this is available for rehire on old and new employments

There is another feature ‘Rehire on New Employment with Future Termination’ and I will be writing a separate article about this.  Once this is published, I will link it here.

Hopefully this blog has summarized the main points from the H2 2026 Onboarding release relating to rehires.

entry.title: Agentic ABAP with MCP: what is really solving problems for you?
entry.content:
With the major update of the ABAP development tools MCP server, MCP for ABAP is no longer an experiment. It now works with Claude Code, Copilot, Codex and the other CLI tools, and many of us already use some kind of agent in daily ABAP work.

I have been building and using agents on top of the ADT REST API for a few months, in my own S/4HANA 2023 lab. Instead of another how-to, I would like to open a discussion: where does it really help, where does it fail, and what could we share as a community? My notes first.

1. The first explanation is often plausible and wrong

This is true for people and for agents. A classic: SQL 305 on a CDS view, "single-row query returns more than one row". The usual explanation is a to-one association that finds duplicates. In my lab that alone gave no error: a LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN from MARA to MAKT, for a material with 3 texts, returned 3 rows. The 305 only came with a scalar subquery that returned more than one row.

What I learned: wherever an explanation comes from, mine or the agent's, it gets reproduced in a sandbox before I believe it. The test is cheap, the wrong explanation is expensive.

2. Reading standard code is where it shines, if you know the limits

Following a call chain through the Gateway runtime classes, to see which DPC methods are really called, is a job of minutes for an agent and of an afternoon for me.

But tools can lie by silence. In my lab, the where-used list of /IWBEP/IF_MGW_CORE_SRV_RUNTIME showed one custom class and none of the SAP classes that I then saw using it in their source. And a text search across packages only covers what it really opened.

What I learned: an empty result is not proof that something doesn't exist. The agent must say what it did not search.

3. The system is the judge, but test the judge first

For code written by a model, I let the system decide: syntax check, ATC, ABAP Unit. Before trusting the judge, I give it two controls: the correct solution must pass, and a known mistake must fail (for example, the language condition in the WHERE instead of the ON of a text join). If the known mistake passes, "it compiles" is quietly becoming "it is right".

4. Context is the real cost

/IWBEP/CL_MGW_ABS_DATA alone has more than 8,000 lines of source. One whole read of a class like this fills a big part of the context, and everything after it gets slower and more expensive. In my own numbers, most of the cost was the model reading a big context again and again, not the answers it wrote. Reading one method, or searching first and reading after, is the habit that pays.

5. Human in the loop, by habit

Read only by default. Writes only in $TMP in my lab, and only after I say yes. Transports stay with a person. It is the same idea as the "safety by default" policy of the SAP server, and I think it is the right default for everybody.

What I would like to hear from you

  1. Which tasks really save you time today: investigation and reading, writing new objects, reviews, tests?
  2. Do you use the official ADT MCP server, a community server, or your own? What made you choose?
  3. How do you check what the agent tells you before you act on it?
  4. How do you deal with authorizations and transports when an agent can write?
  5. What would be worth sharing as a community: AGENTS.md patterns, prompts that work, or a set of "known hard" ABAP questions to test agents on?

If there is interest, I am happy to collect the answers in a follow-up.

entry.title: When Healthcare Transforms. The Foundation Behind Better Decisions.
entry.content:
For us, a Digital Health Platform (DHP) is more than a technology investment. It is the foundation that lets healthcare organizations adapt to change faster, more safely, and more cost-effectively. This two-part series shows how that foundation becomes the operating layer that turns information into action. Part 1 explores the strategic decision. Part 2 shows how that decision is translated into operational reality.

Healthcare markets continuously transform

Across many markets, a combination of structural economic and financial pressure, workforce shortages, and regulatory change is increasing the likelihood that hospitals will close, merge, or transfer services. When that happens, patient flows, workforce availability, referral patterns, and regional competition can shift almost overnight.

Success depends less on anticipating the event and more on responding to it. Organizations need to understand the implications quickly, evaluate their options with confidence, and act while the window for decision-making is still open. For providers operating nearby, a consolidation event can create significant opportunity. Additional patients may require ongoing care, skilled healthcare professionals may become available, and service portfolios can potentially be expanded.

At the same time, important questions must be answered. Does existing capacity support growth? Can operations scale without disruption? Can continuity of care be maintained? And does the opportunity create sustainable value for the organization? For healthcare leaders, this changes the challenge. The question is no longer how to optimize individual processes. It is how to manage an increasingly interconnected ecosystem of patients, providers, partners, and data.

Point solutions rarely solve structural challenges on their own. The organizations best positioned to respond to market change share a common characteristic: they operate from a connected and governed operating backbone. By bringing together clinical, operational, and financial information, they create the conditions for faster decisions, greater resilience, and more effective growth. A Digital Health Platform provides such a foundation. By design, it connects data, processes, and decision-making across the enterprise, enabling organizations to respond to change and act with greater speed and confidence. We see their design as guided by four principles:

The Consolidation Scenario

What follows is illustrative, but reflects the type of decision healthcare organizations are increasingly likely to face as markets transform. Few situations test unification, governance, innovation, and transformation more directly, or reveal more clearly why the foundation beneath the decision matters.

Imagine a hospital nearby announces its closure.

Side by side, the two hospitals appear highly complementary. Your organization brings capacity, financial headroom, and a governed SAP landscape. For illustration, assume the closing hospital brings approximately 4,200 patients in active care, around 320 potentially transferable employees, and a structured patient-record store that can be exported using open interoperability standards, including HL7 FHIR R4.

On paper, the opportunity looks obvious. More patients. Additional clinical talent. Expanded regional relevance. New service-line potential.

But consolidation creates risk at the same speed it creates opportunity. Can your facilities accommodate the additional demand? Can patient records be integrated without compromising continuity of care? Can workforce, finance, and operations scale together? And can all of this be evaluated before competitors move first?

Every board can see the opportunity. The challenge is determining whether the organization can safely and profitably act on it within the decision window available. What separates acquisition from inaction is rarely strategy, it is operational certainty. The board has 72 hours to decide whether to proceed. If the answer is yes, the operational transfer window is 10 to 14 weeks. Within those 72 hours, leadership must answer four questions, each depending on a different form of operational certainty: financial reality, organizational readiness, patient continuity, and resilience at scale. 

The critical requirement is whether the existing foundation can provide sufficient certainty before the decision window closes.  Facts are on the table, the opportunity visible. But visibility is not the same as readiness… What determines the outcome is not the decision itself, but the quality of the data foundation it rests on.

Conditions for Confidence

Four conditions must be addressed within the decision window, each depending on a different form of operational certainty. For organizations already operating on a governed SAP landscape, much of this does not require a new foundation. Much of the data, processes, and architecture needed to assess each condition is likely already in place:

The board is now in a position to make a robust decision: proceed, pause, or reject. Not because the future is certain, because the variables that matter are no longer invisible.

  • Break-even & margin outlook, and investment need
  • Organizational readiness gaps
  • Patient continuity gaps
  • Resilience & sustainability at scale

Each condition addressed, each answer drawn from the organization’s own operational reality. That is what a governed SAP landscape makes possible.

Most Healthcare Organizations Are Closer Than They Think

 

None of these conditions are built overnight. They emerge from years of investment in ERP, revenue cycle and analytics, process management, enterprise architecture, data integration, and AI. For many organizations already running SAP, that groundwork is further along than it might appear. The distance varies: some already operate on cloud ERP with a governed data foundation, while others are still navigating the S/4HANA transition. The direction is the same in both cases.

The capabilities themselves are rarely missing. SAP S/4HANA provides operational and financial ground truth. LeanIX documents technology reality. Signavio captures process reality. SAP Business Data Cloud, including SAP Datasphere, connects information across domains. Joule provides a natural way to interact with all of it, a capability that deepens as the platform evolves. What is often missing is the connection between them.

The move, therefore, is not to build a new platform. It is to bundle, extend, and connect what already exists into one intelligence layer, and the skills to do so are largely in place. Because such a platform is modular, it also shifts more architectural responsibility to the organization itself, which is why governance and enterprise architecture belong at its center.

Connected this way, the landscape becomes a Digital Health Platform: not another system, but the operating layer that links the realities an organization already manages separately (clinical, operational, financial, and architectural) and turns them into coordinated action. For most organizations, the path is evolutionary rather than disruptive, and it is one way healthcare organizations move toward what SAP calls the Autonomous Enterprise.

So when the next consolidation event arrives, data is less likely to be the constraint. What matters is whether the organization can turn that data into execution before the window closes. Organizations that can do so act with confidence. Those that cannot often respond with hesitation.

What Is Coming Next

Part 1 established the conditions for confidence and showed that required capabilities largely exist. A robust decision is within reach. What follows is harder. Not the decision, the delivery.

Part 2 (coming soon) goes inside execution.

  • How patient records are integrated before patients arrive.
  • How workforce, finance, and operations scale together.
  • How a board decision turns into operational reality.

entry.title: Natural Language (NL) Over SAP Data: A Practical MCP Pattern for Joule Desktop & Pro-Code Agent
entry.content:
Introduction

Any S/4HANA OData API, standard or custom, can be exposed as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway and consumed by AI agents through two complementary paths: Joule Work Desktop for a direct, low-overhead experience, and a custom agent in Cloud Foundry that can be triggered in Joule SAP Build Work Zone for an orchestrated, reasoning-capable experience. 

To make it concrete, we applied it to SAP Production Revenue Accounting (PRA) data: a domain that is rich, complex, and mission-critical, and where the gap between the data and the people who need it is wide enough to make the pattern's value immediately visible. The solution is not PRA-specific. The same architecture applies to any standard or custom OData V4 service in S/4HANA: Finance, Plant Maintenance, Materials Management, Sales and Distribution, or any domain where business users need structured answers without writing queries or navigating transaction codes.

This blog walks through the architecture, the components, the implementation decisions, and the trade-offs behind the two access patterns we designed and deployed:

  1. Joule Work Desktop — connects directly to an custom MCP server published via SAP Integration Suite. Ideal for business users who want a direct AI interface to standard PRA revenue accounting tables.

  2. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone — routes through a custom AI agent on SAP Cloud Foundry that adds an intelligent reasoning layer. Ideal for business users already operating inside Work Zone.

Both patterns share the same backend: a custom OData V4 service exposing standard SAP PRA tables, published as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway.

A full end-to-end walkthrough has been recorded as a companion to this blog.

Solution Architecture

The architecture is deliberately generic. Swap out the PRA OData service for any other S/4HANA OData V4 endpoint and the rest of the pattern holds unchanged.

The solution exposes standard S/4HANA PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service (built on ABAP RAP), publishes them as governed MCP tools through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway, and surfaces them to business users via natural language either directly through Joule Work Desktop or through a custom AI agent embedded in SAP Build Work Zone.

Path 1 — Joule Desktop:

Desktop User → Joule Desktop → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Path 2 — Joule in Work Zone:

Web User → SAP Build Work Zone (Joule) → A2A → Custom Agent on CF → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Component Walkthrough

1. S/4HANA On-Premise — The Data Source

The data lives in a standard S/4HANA on-premise system. We exposed the standard PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service built using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The service exposes all 13 entity sets with proper navigation associations, enabling deep $expand queries across both the Document and Revenue Distribution branches. 

 

2. SAP Integration Suite — MCP Gateway

This is the integration layer that bridges the RAP OData service into the AI world.

SAP Integration Suite's MCP Server capability (part of the MCP Gateway feature, available with the Premium subscription) consumes the OData V4 service metadata and automatically generates MCP tool definitions for every operation. For our 13-entity service, this produced 41 MCP tools covering list queries, filtered reads, and navigation operations.

Why MCP? The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for AI tool discovery and invocation. By publishing our OData service as an MCP server, we make it consumable by any MCP-compatible client, including Joule Work Desktop, LangChain agents, or any future client, without changing the backend.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

The Developer Hub within Integration Suite is used to publish the MCP server, generating the OAuth credentials that clients use to authenticate. It also provides discoverability within the organization: other developers can find and reuse the same MCP server without rebuilding the integration from scratch.

3. SAP Cloud Foundry — Custom Reasoning Agent

For the Work Zone path, we built a custom Python agent deployed on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry. This agent adds the reasoning layer that bridges Joule's natural language input to structured MCP tool calls.

The agent stack:

ComponentRole

a2a-sdk

Implements the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, exposing a JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint that Joule can call

LangGraph + LangChain

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) loop: decides which MCP tools to call, in what order, based on the user's question

langchain-mcp-adapters

Loads MCP tools from Integration Suite at runtime and wraps them as LangChain 

LiteLLM / langchain-litellm

Routes LLM calls to SAP AI Core using the standard OpenAI-compatible interface

The ReAct pattern is important here. Rather than a single-shot query, the agent reasons iteratively: it reads the question, identifies which MCP tools are relevant, calls them, evaluates the results, and decides whether additional calls are needed before formulating the final answer. This is what makes it capable of answering multi-hop questions that require joining data from multiple PRA tables.

4. Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

Deployment uses the Joule CLI. The deploy command registers the custom agent as a Joule capability. By default, this deploys to standalone Joule.

To surface the agent inside SAP Build Work Zone, update the assistant type to sap_digital_Assistant. The Joule Admin Center (accessible by appending /admin to the Joule instance URL) allows you to verify the deployment and confirm the capability is active.

5. SAP Build Work Zone - Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

SAP Build Work Zone is the standard business user entry point. Joule is embedded natively in the Work Zone shell,  no separate app to open, no separate login.

6. Joule Work Desktop Experience

For users who prefer the Joule Work Desktop standalone experience, the integration is simpler: Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server. No custom agent, no A2A, no Cloud Foundry deployment required.

Conclusion

The architecture supports two distinct experiences from the same foundation. Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server no agent required giving business users a fast, lightweight path to query SAP data in natural language. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone routes through a custom AI agent deployed on BTP Cloud Foundry, adding multi-step reasoning, tool orchestration, and a governed conversational interface for broader business user adoption.

The architecture is composable by design. The OData V4 service, MCP server, reasoning agent, and Joule capability are independent layers each doing one thing well. Swap the data source and the pattern applies to any SAP domain. Complexity lives where it belongs: the OData layer owns the data model, MCP handles tool discoverability, LangGraph handles reasoning, and Joule handles the conversation.

Consider which of your OData APIs could benefit from this pattern  a Finance posting service, a Plant Maintenance feed, a Sales Order status endpoint. Any of them can become a natural language interface using exactly this stack.

Guidance Along the Implementation Journey

The SAP Sustainability Control Tower End-to-End Implementation Guide was created to support project teams throughout an implementation. It is a comprehensive guide for ESG projects with SAP Sustainability Control Tower.

entry.title: Re: How does AI fit into a clean core strategy for S/4HAN...
entry.content:
Hi @thanoj_y ,

In a clean core strategy for SAP S/4HANA, AI should be integrated in a way that preserves the stability of the core while enabling innovation and flexibility.

  • SAP BTP side-by-side: This is generally the preferred place for custom AI logic, orchestration, integrations with external AI services, and custom applications. It keeps AI dependencies outside the S/4HANA core and allows models to evolve independently.
  • Inside the S/4HANA stack: Keep core business rules, transactional validations, and essential business logic in S/4HANA using released APIs and supported extension mechanisms such as ABAP Cloud and released extension points. Avoid modifications to standard SAP objects.
  • SAP Joule: Use Joule for conversational experiences, natural-language interaction, and AI-assisted business workflows where standard SAP capabilities meet the requirement. Extend it with custom skills or integrations when needed, rather than embedding all AI logic in the user interface.

How to keep AI extensions upgrade-safe:

  1. Use released APIs, events, and extension points instead of accessing internal SAP objects.
  2. Isolate model providers and AI services behind well-defined interfaces so that models can be replaced without changing core business logic.
  3. Validate AI outputs before they trigger business transactions. Use deterministic business rules, authorization checks, and human approval for high-impact decisions.
  4. Handle timeouts, failures, model changes, and inconsistent outputs through retries, fallbacks, versioning, monitoring, and regression testing.
  5. Keep AI prompts, configurations, and orchestration independently deployable and test extensions against S/4HANA upgrades.

My recommendation: Keep S/4HANA as the system of record, use SAP BTP as the primary home for custom AI orchestration and side-by-side extensions, and use Joule as the conversational entry point where appropriate. This separation supports clean core principles, reduces upgrade risks, and allows AI capabilities to evolve without tightly coupling them to the ERP core.

entry.title: Re: How do you measure the business value of an SAP AI us...
entry.content:
Hi @MD-Saad_1634,
Measuring the business value of an SAP AI use case after go-live requires comparing actual results against a clearly defined pre-implementation baseline.

I would focus on five key KPIs:

  • Time saved: Reduction in processing time per transaction or task.
  • Error reduction: Fewer manual errors, rework cases, and incorrect postings.
  • Adoption rate: Percentage of eligible users or transactions actively using the AI solution.
  • Cost per transaction: Total operating cost, including AI consumption, integration, infrastructure, and support, divided by transactions processed.
  • Business impact: Improvement in productivity, cycle time, customer satisfaction, compliance, or revenue, depending on the use case.

How I would measure the value:

  1. Establish a baseline: Capture 4–8 weeks of pre-go-live data, including transaction volumes, average processing time, error rates, and operational costs.
  2. Define success criteria: Agree with business sponsors on measurable targets before implementation, such as reducing invoice-processing time by 30% or manual effort by 25%.
  3. Track post-go-live performance: Monitor KPIs at 30, 60, and 90 days, using SAP reports, process analytics, application logs, and AI usage metrics as appropriate.
  4. Validate actual benefits: Compare results with the baseline while accounting for transaction volumes, seasonality, process changes, and other factors. Where possible, use a comparable control group.
  5. Calculate ROI: Compare verified financial benefits with implementation and ongoing operating costs.

For example, if an AI solution saves 5 minutes per transaction across 10,000 transactions per month, it saves approximately 833 hours monthly. I would translate those hours into financial value only after validating how much of that capacity is actually converted into cost savings, additional throughput, or productive work.

Finally, I would present a monthly business-value dashboard to sponsors showing baseline versus actual performance, adoption, realized savings, total cost of ownership, ROI, and outstanding improvement actions.

The key principle is that AI success should be measured by measurable business outcomes—not just model accuracy, technical performance, or the number of users who tried the feature.

entry.title: Re: How do you secure AI agents that call SAP APIs and MC...
entry.content:
Hi @MD-Saad_1634 ,

Securing AI agents that call SAP APIs and MCP servers requires treating the agent as an untrusted orchestrator, not as a trusted user. The key is to ensure that every action is authenticated, authorized, and auditable.

My recommended approach is to focus on five controls:

  1. Identity propagation: Use SAP Cloud Identity Services and supported OAuth 2.0 flows to authenticate users and propagate their identity to downstream services wherever supported. Avoid sharing user credentials or relying on a single technical account for all users. If delegated identity cannot be propagated, explicitly define the agent's service identity and restrict its permissions.
  2. Least-privilege access: Grant access only to the APIs, business objects, and operations required for the use case. Enforce authorization in the SAP backend, not just in the agent or prompt. Separate read operations from write operations and require additional approval for sensitive transactions.
  3. Secure API and MCP access: Place API Management or an equivalent gateway in front of exposed services where appropriate. Enforce token validation, scopes, rate limits, input validation, and allowlisted tools. For MCP servers, authenticate clients, authorize individual tools, validate arguments, and restrict access to approved endpoints. Never assume that an MCP tool is safe simply because it is registered.
  4. Auditability: Log the initiating user, agent identity, delegated or service identity, tool invoked, target API, timestamp, authorization decision, and transaction outcome. Use correlation IDs to trace a request across the agent, gateway, MCP server, and SAP backend. Avoid logging access tokens, credentials, or unnecessary sensitive business data.
  5. Human approval and runtime safeguards: Require confirmation for high-impact actions such as posting payments, changing vendor bank details, or deleting business records. Add transaction limits, idempotency controls, timeouts, and protections against prompt injection and malicious tool responses.

Architecture recommendation: Use SAP Cloud Identity Services for identity and federation, SAP API Management or an equivalent gateway for API-level controls, and SAP backend authorization for final access decisions. For Joule Studio or custom agents, use the supported identity and authorization mechanisms of the chosen runtime rather than assuming that every integration supports transparent user delegation.

One important lesson is that authentication alone does not establish authorization. An agent may have a valid token and still attempt an action the user should not be allowed to perform. Therefore, enforce permissions at every trust boundary and maintain an end-to-end audit trail that links the user's request to the actual business transaction.

I would also test explicitly for confused-deputy scenarios, privilege escalation, replayed requests, prompt injection, and service-account overreach before production rollout.

entry.title: Re: ABAP syntax advice
entry.content:
Hi @jeff_broodwar,

Thanks for the mention. The others already showed that the short and the long lines do different things. One part is still open: why the [] is there at all.

SELECT-OPTIONS s_bukrs creates a table with a header line: two data objects with the same name, the table body and one work area. Your gt_bukrs (TYPE RANGE OF bukrs) has no header line. The ABAP Keyword Documentation (Internal Tables with a Header Line) gives the rule:

  • In most operand positions, s_bukrs alone is the header line (one row). s_bukrs[] is the table.
  • Where only a table makes sense, s_bukrs is already the table: LOOP AT s_bukrs, and after FOR ... IN.
  • For a table without a header line, [] is allowed but changes nothing. A field symbol also points to only one of the two, so <fs_bukrs>[] is the same as <fs_bukrs>.

So with your declarations:

gt_bukrs = s_bukrs[].                 "[] only because s_bukrs has a header line
LOOP AT s_bukrs INTO DATA(ls_bukrs).  "here s_bukrs is already the table

That is why sample 3 needs no [] after IN s_bukrs, and why gt_bukrs[] = and r_bukrs[] = are the same as gt_bukrs = and r_bukrs =.

About taking only LOW (samples 1 and 3): with a range as target it gives wrong rows, as TMNielsen showed. Even into a plain TABLE OF bukrs it changes the selection: intervals (BT), excludes (E) and patterns (CP) are lost. And an empty select-option means "all": the documentation of IN range_tab says "If the ranges table is initial, the expression IN range_tab is always true". A list of LOW values from an empty select-option is just an empty list.

What I do is keep the range and use it directly in the WHERE (WHERE bukrs IN @s_bukrs). When I really need the single values, I let the database resolve the range against T001:

SELECT bukrs FROM t001 WHERE bukrs IN @s_bukrs INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_bukrs).

entry.title: Blog 9 - SAP ESM for HR - UAT: How to Test SAP ESM for HR Before You Go Live
entry.content:
The Phase That Always Gets Compressed

Ask any project manager on a delayed SAP ESM implementation what happens to the UAT phase when the schedule slips, and you will get the same answer: it gets compressed. Scope gets reduced, test cycles get shortened, defects get deferred, and teams convince themselves that what does not get tested in UAT will get caught in production.

It will. And it will be far more expensive to fix.

UAT — User Acceptance Testing — is the last structured opportunity to validate that everything you have designed, configured, and integrated actually works as intended, end to end, in a realistic environment, with real HR scenarios. It is not a technical check. It is a business validation. And done well, it is what separates a confident go-live from a nervous one.

This post gives you the framework to do it well.

What UAT in ESM Is — and What It Is No

A common mistake is treating ESM UAT as a feature checklist: "Can I create a case? Can I close a case? Can I search the knowledge base?" That approach will pass most scenarios and miss most of the real risks.

UAT for SAP ESM for HR is the validation of **end-to-end workflows** across all configured channels, categories, routing rules, SLA timers, integrations, and user roles, under realistic conditions, performed by the people who will use the system on day one.

The question you are answering is not "does the system work?" It is: "does the system work the way our HR operation needs it to, for every scenario that will arrive on day one?"

That is a materially different test.

Who Needs to Be in the UAT Team

UAT is not an IT activity. It is a joint business and IT activity, and the business must lead it.

The UAT team for an ESM for HR implementation should include:

| Role | Responsibility in UAT |

  • | **HR Agents (Tier 1)** | Test case creation, routing receipt, case processing, response templates, SLA visibility |
  • | **HR Specialists (Tier 2)** | Test escalated case handling, complex category workflows, direct-to-Tier-2 routing |
  • | **HR Managers / Supervisors** | Test supervisor views, SLA dashboards, escalation notifications, team workload visibility |
  • | **IT / Integration team** | Test SuccessFactors data validation, outbound transaction execution, IAS/SSO, BTP connectivity |
  • | **Employees (pilot group)** | Test the self-service portal, case submission, status tracking, email acknowledgement receipt |
  • | **UAT Coordinator** | Manages the test script, logs defects, tracks sign-off, coordinates the go/no-go decision |

The employee pilot group is the component most commonly omitted from UAT. This is a significant gap. HR agents can test the agent workspace all day, but only an actual employee can validate what the self-service experience feels like — whether the portal is navigable, whether the category options make sense, and whether the confirmation emails are clear.

Minimum recommended pilot group size: 10–15 employees drawn from different countries, departments, and seniority levels if your rollout is global.

The Five Test Scenario Types

A well-structured ESM for HR UAT covers five distinct scenario types. Each tests a different layer of the implementation. Missing any one of them leaves a class of risk untested.

Scenario Type 1 — Case Creation by Channel

What you are testing: That every configured inbound channel correctly creates a case, assigns it the right category, applies the right employee context, and routes it to the right team.

Test scenarios to include:

  • Employee submits a case via the self-service portal (standard category, correct country)
  • Employee emails the **HR mailbox** — case auto-creates with correct subject mapping and employee lookup
  • HR agent manually creates a case on behalf of an employee (walk-in / phone call scenario)
  • Employee uses SAP Joule — question answered from knowledge base (deflection success), and question not answered — case created automatically (deflection failure → case creation)

What to look for:

  • Does the employee's SuccessFactors profile load correctly in the case context?
  • Is the auto-acknowledgement email sent within the configured time (best practice: 5 minutes)?
  • Does the case land in the correct Agent Group queue?
  • Is the category pre-populated correctly for email-created cases?

Scenario Type 2 — Routing Validation

What you are testing: That every case category routes to the correct HR team, under every combination of employee country and org unit that is in scope.

This is the most labour-intensive scenario type because it requires you to test the routing matrix — every category × every country combination — not just a representative sample. Routing errors are silent in the system: the case creates without error, it just lands with the wrong team.

Test scenarios to include:

  • Same category submitted by employees in three different countries — verify different Agent Group assignment
  • Category that should route directly to Tier 2 (e.g., Employee Relations) — verify it bypasses Tier 1 entirely
  • Category submitted by an indirect employee (non-SuccessFactors EC) — verify fallback routing behaviour
  • Case submitted outside business hours — verify correct handling (queued, auto-reply, or out-of-hours team)

What to look for:

  • Does every category × country combination route to the expected team?
  • Is the direct-to-Tier-2 routing behaving correctly for complex categories?
  • What happens when the routing rule finds no match? Is there a safe fallback?

Scenario Type 3 — SLA Configuration

What you are testing: That SLA timers start correctly, business hours are applied accurately, warning notifications fire at the configured threshold, and breach notifications trigger on time.

SLA testing is frequently under-tested because testers do not want to wait for real-time timers to expire. The solution is to use test SLA configurations with compressed timers (e.g., 5-minute resolution SLA instead of 8-hour) in the UAT environment — then revert to production values before go-live.

Test scenarios to include:

  • Create a case and verify the SLA milestone fields populate with the correct due timestamps
  • Let a case approach the warning threshold — verify the warning notification fires to the correct recipient
  • Let a case breach — verify the breach notification fires, and any configured escalation actions execute (reassignment, priority change, supervisor notification)
  • Create a case outside business hours — verify the SLA timer does not count non-business hours
  • Test a public holiday calendar — verify the SLA timer pauses correctly on a configured holiday

What to look for:

  • Do SLA milestone timestamps reflect the correct business hours calculation?
  • Do warning and breach notifications reach the right recipients?
  • Does the escalation action (reassignment, priority change) execute correctly at breach?
  • Are public holidays and time zones handled correctly for each in-scope country?

Scenario Type 4 — SAP SuccessFactors Integration

What you are testing: That the integration between ESM and SuccessFactors works correctly in both directions — inbound employee data validation and outbound transaction automation.

This is the highest-risk scenario type in terms of go-live impact. An integration failure on day one affects every case, not just edge cases.

Test scenarios to include:

  • Submit a case as an active employee — verify the full SuccessFactors employee profile loads in the case context (name, employee ID, country, company code, org unit, manager, employment status)
  • Submit a case using an inactive employee ID — verify the system handles the lookup gracefully (error message, fallback behaviour)
  • If outbound transactions are in scope: trigger an automated HR transaction from a case (e.g., address change, leave request) — verify the transaction executes correctly in SuccessFactors and the case is updated with the outcome
  • Verify SSO: log in as an employee via the self-service portal — confirm no separate login is required
  • Verify IAS role propagation: log in as each user role (employee, HR agent, HR supervisor, HR administrator) — confirm each sees only what they should see and can perform only the actions they should be able to perform

What to look for:

  • Is the employee data lookup fast enough to be acceptable in production? (More than 3 seconds is a usability concern)
  • Are all expected SuccessFactors fields visible in the ESM case context?
  • Do outbound transactions execute without errors, and are they reflected correctly in SuccessFactors?
  • Does SSO work without prompting for credentials?

Scenario Type 5 — End-to-End Lifecycle

What you are testing: The full lifecycle of an HR case — from submission by an employee, through routing, agent processing, escalation if needed, resolution, employee notification, and case closure — across several representative scenarios.

This is the most important test type because it validates the system as a whole, not its individual components. It is also the scenario type most likely to surface integration and configuration gaps that were not visible in isolated tests.

Representative end-to-end scenarios to include:

  • Standard query resolved at Tier 1:

Employee submits payslip query via portal → routed to Payroll team → HR agent responds → employee receives notification → case closed → CSAT survey sent (if configured)

  • Query escalated from Tier 1 to Tier 2:

Employee submits query via email → Tier 1 agent reviews and escalates → case reassigned to Tier 2 specialist → specialist resolves → employee notified → case closed

  • Direct-to-Tier-2 complex case:

Employee submits an Employee Relations query → routes directly to ER specialist → specialist processes → case closed with internal notes

  • SLA breach scenario:

Case created → not actioned within SLA window → warning fires → breach occurs → escalation notification sent to supervisor → supervisor reassigns → case resolved

  • Joule deflection scenario:

Employee asks a question via Joule → answer provided from knowledge base → no case created → employee confirms resolved

How to Structure Your UAT Script

A UAT script is more than a list of steps. Each test case should contain six elements:

| Element | Description |

  1. | **Test Case ID** | Unique identifier (e.g., UAT-CH-001 for channel tests) |
  2. | **Scenario Description** | Plain-language description of what is being tested and why |
  3. | **Prerequisites** | What must be true before the test can start (user logged in, test employee ID available, etc.) |
  4. | **Step-by-step test actions** | Exactly what the tester does, in sequence |
  5. | **Expected result** | Precisely what the system should do — not "it works" but "case routes to Payroll EMEA Agent Group within 30 seconds with employee profile loaded" |
  6. | **Pass / Fail / Deferred** | The outcome, with space for the tester to add notes |

The level of precision in the expected result is what separates a useful UAT script from a useless one. "System behaves correctly" is not an expected result. "Case appears in the Payroll EMEA Agent Group queue within 60 seconds, with employee name, employee ID, and country populated from SuccessFactors EC" is.

Defect Classification: What Is a Blocker?

Not every defect found in UAT should block go-live. The decision about what to fix before go-live and what to defer requires a clear classification framework. Use a three-tier approach:

P1 — Go-live blocker:

  • Any defect that prevents a case from being created, routed, or processed
  • Any SSO or IAS failure that prevents users from accessing the system
  • Any SuccessFactors integration failure that causes incorrect employee data
  • Any SLA misconfiguration that causes incorrect due dates
  • Any routing error that sends cases to the wrong team

P2 — Fix before go-live, non-blocking:

  • Notification email formatting issues
  • Minor UI/label discrepancies
  • Knowledge base article content errors
  • Non-critical report configuration issues

P3 — Defer to post go-live:

  • Cosmetic issues with no functional impact
  • Nice-to-have configuration improvements
  • Reporting enhancements
  • Additional knowledge base articles

The discipline is in enforcing the P1 definition. There is always pressure to accept P1 defects with workarounds. Resist it. A go-live with broken routing or a broken integration is not a go-live — it is a controlled incident.

The Go/No-Go Decision

The go/no-go decision should be made by a defined group — typically the project sponsor, the HR SSC lead, and the IT/integration lead — based on explicit, pre-agreed criteria. Do not improvise this decision in a meeting the day before go-live.

Go-live criteria — all must be true:

  • [ ] All P1 defects resolved and re-tested
  • [ ] All five scenario types completed with a pass rate of ≥ 95%
  • [ ] SuccessFactors integration validated with at least three different employee profiles per in-scope country
  • [ ] SSO tested successfully for all user roles
  • [ ] SLA timers validated for all in-scope categories and countries
  • [ ] At least one full end-to-end lifecycle scenario completed per in-scope country
  • [ ] HR agents and supervisors have confirmed readiness (formal sign-off)
  • [ ] Cutover plan reviewed and approved (see Blog 10)
  • [ ] Hypercare team identified and available from day one

If any of these criteria are not met, the go/no-go decision should be a no-go, with a clear action plan and revised date.

Common UAT Mistakes

Starting UAT too late. UAT should begin no later than three weeks before the planned go-live date. Starting with one week to go leaves no time to fix P1 defects, re-test, and make a confident go/no-go decision.

Testing with fictional data. Use real SuccessFactors employee records (from a test or sandbox environment) in UAT. Testing with invented employee IDs that do not exist in SuccessFactors will not surface integration issues.

Only involving IT in the integration tests. HR operations staff must participate in integration testing. They are the ones who will notice if the employee profile data is incomplete or if an automated transaction produces incorrect results.

Not testing failure scenarios. What happens when SuccessFactors is temporarily unavailable? What happens when an email arrives with an unknown sender? What happens when a case is submitted in a language not currently in the knowledge base? Failure path testing is as important as happy path testing.

Deferring the employee pilot. The self-service portal UAT with real employees is consistently the test that produces the most unexpected feedback — not because of configuration errors, but because of usability and language issues that no amount of internal testing will surface.

Treating UAT sign-off as a formality. If stakeholders sign off on UAT without having actively participated in testing, the sign-off is meaningless. HR agent team leads and the HR SSC manager should be able to look at the test results and say "I tested this myself and it works."

UAT Readiness Checklist

Before UAT begins, the following must be true:

  • [ ] UAT environment is fully configured and connected to SuccessFactors sandbox
  • [ ] Test employee IDs are available for all in-scope countries
  • [ ] All user accounts (employee, HR agent, HR supervisor, HR administrator) are provisioned and accessible
  • [ ] IAS and SSO are configured in the UAT environment
  • [ ] UAT test script is finalised and distributed to all testers
  • [ ] UAT coordinator and defect log are in place
  • [ ] SLA timers have been adjusted to compressed values for testing
  • [ ] Joule is configured and connected to the test knowledge base (if in scope for Wave 1)
  • [ ] Email channel is connected to a test mailbox
  • [ ] Go/no-go criteria are documented and agreed by all stakeholders

What Comes Next

A successful UAT does not mean you are ready to go live. It means you are ready to plan the cutover — the 72-hour sequence of activities that takes the system from a tested UAT state to a live production environment, with HR agents trained, employees notified, and the hypercare team standing by.
