entry.title: My ABAP Escaped the Server, Or: Everything Gets Better with Go.
entry.content:
Or: Everything Gets Better with Go.

TL;DR: ABAP report on ZX Spectrum, CP/M, MOS AgonLight (ez80), and a mac.

I like JavaScript, and TypeScript too. JavaScript has become something of a lingua franca of modern computing, rather like BASIC was in the eighties: back then you could walk up to almost any home computer and find a BASIC interpreter waiting for you, and although the machines were different, the dialects were different, and sometimes even the meaning of PRINT was a matter of local tradition, you could usually get something running. Today it's JavaScript — in browsers, servers, desktop applications, little embedded environments, and places where you might reasonably wonder who invited it.

I love being able to take an idea and run it almost anywhere, and TypeScript makes the whole arrangement much more comfortable once the idea grows beyond a few hundred lines. But I also love Go. There is something deeply satisfying about compiling a program into a native executable, copying that one file to another machine and watching it run, without a dependency installation ceremony, a carefully reconstructed development environment, or a server that must be started beforehand.

After spending the last couple of months getting ABAP to run outside SAP with Open SteamGate, I began to wonder whether we could go a little further. OSG could already run ABAP locally, serve OData, work with CDS and connect to Eclipse, and I wrote an entire article about how a simple experiment had grown into something resembling an application server.

But what if I didn't need an application server at all, and just wanted to run a report? A perfectly ordinary ABAP report, with PARAMETERS, SELECT-OPTIONS, a selection screen, some Open SQL, a little file processing and WRITE statements at the end. Could I compile it into an executable and run it in my terminal — not start a server, not install a runtime, not connect to a development system, just run the program, and preferably have it stop when it finishes?

Well, yes, as it turns out. And then the terminal started acquiring features. 😃

The report that acquired a terminal

Let me show you where this ended up.

This is an ABAP report compiled into a native executable by osabap, part of Open SteamGate's new ABAP-to-Go compiler. The report still has its PARAMETERS and SELECT-OPTIONS, its INITIALIZATION and START-OF-SELECTION events are still there, and WRITE still produces the output; but instead of opening a selection screen in SAP GUI, the program renders it as a form in the terminal, where you can move between fields, edit values, toggle checkboxes and execute the report. The source is ABAP, and the result is a native executable.

I rather like command-line tools, so the next thing I wanted was to run the same report without the interactive screen. Parameters become command-line options, a checkbox becomes a flag, and SELECT-OPTIONS can be given as repeated values or as ranges. WRITE output goes to stdout, messages go to stderr, and the process returns an exit status that another program can understand, so the report can sit in a shell pipeline, a scheduled job or a CI run.

A classic ABAP report had become a CLI tool. The funny thing is that the report itself doesn't need to know about any of this: we haven't rewritten its business logic in a special command-line language. The compiler takes the report and its supported dependencies, produces Go, and builds an executable that carries the runtime it needs, so neither Go nor Node is required on the machine that runs it — both belong to the build. This is a growing implementation of a supported ABAP subset, not a promise that every report from every SAP system will compile unchanged; but for the reports that do compile, it is a rather different way of deploying ABAP, and quite a pleasant way of running it.

Naturally, I pressed F4

Once the terminal selection screen worked, I started doing what an ABAP developer does with a selection screen, and almost immediately I pressed F4. Of course I did.

If a report asks for a filename, you don't really want to type the whole path into a terminal field, and ABAP already has a perfectly good way of offering values for a field: AT SELECTION-SCREEN ON VALUE-REQUEST. So why not let it work in the terminal too?

And there it is. The terminal form calls the report's value-request event; when the report uses one of the supported frontend file dialogs, the terminal opens a file browser, you move with the arrow keys, filter with /, choose with Enter, and the chosen path goes back into the ABAP parameter as though this were a perfectly normal thing for it to do. The same machinery covers the file-open, file-save and directory-browse calls of CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES, within the supported terminal implementation.

There was one rather important question, though: now that the report could browse files on my computer, which files should it be allowed to see? The answer is only the directories explicitly granted to it, with reading and writing granted separately. The browser lists the permitted roots, and the DATASET implementation applies the same sandbox when the ABAP code actually opens a file, including paths it constructs without the browser. A file chooser that politely hides a forbidden directory is not much of a security boundary if OPEN DATASET can simply read it anyway, so F4 didn't just need a pretty interface; it needed to agree with the file-access rules underneath it.

 

The result is a native terminal application whose user interface is still described by an ABAP report. You can even serve the selection screen to a real SAP GUI over a local DIAG connection, although that is a separate, limited frontend mode, and the terminal F4 browser belongs to the terminal form, not to it.

So we started with a command-line executable, and it had now acquired a selection screen, value help, a SQLite database when the report has tables of its own, and access to files under explicit permissions. This was beginning to feel familiar. Fortunately, it could still exit when the report finished, which was becoming an important design feature.

The implementation and examples are described in osabap, and the F4 implementation has its own documentation.

But how did ABAP become Go?

The nice thing about working on top of Lars Hvam Petersen's abaplint ecosystem is that we didn't have to start by teaching a new parser the ABAP language: abaplint already understands an extraordinary amount of ABAP syntax and structure, and its transpiler already handles expression precedence and many of the language's complications. I wanted to reuse that knowledge rather than reproduce it, and at first the idea sounded like simply adding another backend: where the existing transpiler produces JavaScript, ours would produce Go.

This is easier to say than to do. JavaScript, Go and ABAP have rather different ideas about values, types and operations, and you cannot translate a method call into a Go method call and hope that everything around it behaves correctly. In ABAP the receiving type can decide how an expression is evaluated, so computing with the obvious Go types and converting the answer afterwards may already be the wrong calculation; moving values between structures has its own semantics; internal tables are not quite slices; references and method-local data have lifetimes that don't map neatly onto Go declarations; and, of course, there is SY, because there always is.

So the interesting part became the layer in between: a typed intermediate representation, or IR, in which the frontend has already decided what each operation means. The calculation type is known and conversions are explicit, so the backend doesn't look at an expression and improvise an interpretation of ABAP — it expresses a decision that has already been made. The path is roughly:

ABAP → abaplint parser → typed IR → Go → native executable

The frontend reuses abaplint’s parser and the transpiler’s precedence pass, then makes every ABAP decision once, in gogen’s typed IR. Two emitters spell that IR as Go or as JavaScript. From Go come two kinds of program: one report as a native command, or OSGo, open-steamgate’s own ABAP runtime compiled into one server binary.

Sources: tools/gogen/README.md “Shape” and “Language or model?”, docs/osabap-native.md, docs/osgo-release.md (“OSGo does not serve ADT yet”).

The generated Go uses a runtime library for the ABAP behaviours that don't belong to Go's language model, such as internal tables, conversion rules and session state. Once we had this representation, we could test it against the original ABAP behaviour, including recordings from a real SAP system, which mattered, because a compiler that produces a wrong answer very quickly has not improved the situation very much.

I would love to say that we got every rule right on the first attempt. We did not. Some of the differences were small enough to fit in the last bit of a floating-point value, and others were visible in whole frames of an animation: you might remember the mountains and the rotating tesseract from the previous article, and drawing the output turned out to be a remarkably effective way of noticing when two runtimes disagreed about arithmetic. Once the Go backend produced correct results for the tested subset, we started measuring.

Everything gets better with Go. Or does it?

The first numbers were encouraging. On a recursive Fibonacci workload the generated Go took about 0.24 ms, against roughly 24 ms through the existing transpiled JavaScript — about a hundred times faster — and a million-row internal-table workload showed a large difference too.

I am quite happy to accept arguments in favour of Go, but a hundredfold difference on such an ordinary workload is worth examining before declaring one language a hundred times better than another, because V8 is an enormously sophisticated piece of engineering. When we looked, much of the cost wasn't JavaScript at all; it was the execution model. In the existing transpiler output, ABAP values are runtime objects, arithmetic goes through the runtime's operations, and every method call is asynchronous, with async and await throughout the generated code. These are sensible choices for a general runtime that must emulate ABAP, but in a recursive workload each tiny call carries that machinery with it.

Our new IR had already worked out the types, conversions and operations, so we tried emitting JavaScript from the same IR, with plain values where the semantics allow it and synchronous calls. And here is the part I particularly enjoyed: the new JavaScript was dramatically faster too. Fibonacci went from about 24 ms in the transpiled JavaScript to 0.96 ms in JavaScript generated from the IR, and to 0.24 ms in Go, so Go was still ahead, but by about four times rather than a hundred; the million-row table went from 311 ms to 11.3 ms, against 8.7 ms in Go. Across the measured workloads, the new JavaScript path was roughly 7–28 times faster than the original transpiler output.

We set out to make ABAP faster with Go, and found how to make it much faster in JavaScript first. The same typed IR emitted as JavaScript, with plain values and synchronous calls, takes Fibonacci(25) from 24 ms to under 1 ms; Go adds the last step. One machine, two programs, not a ranking of languages.

Source: tools/gogen/README.md, “Language or model? The same IR emitted as JS” (measured 2026-09-23; 16-core x86-64 WSL2, Node 26.9, Go 1.26.0). The README has two more workloads (primes, a table of 10⁶ rows) with the same pattern.

These are measurements of particular programs and runtime versions, not a universal language ranking, and the gogen research notes contain the workloads, the environment and the numbers. What interested me was the explanation: the biggest improvement came from moving decisions into the compiler, instead of making the runtime work them out again and again.

Because the same IR can be emitted as both Go and JavaScript, we now also had two implementations to compare with each other and with SAP. Agreement between two backends is useful evidence, but the original ABAP behaviour remains the reference, since independent implementations can make independent mistakes.

There was one more twist: we compiled the Go to WebAssembly and ran it in a browser, and for the measured rendering workloads the IR-generated JavaScript was faster than Go/WASM, partly because the latter carries a larger runtime and different execution costs. So after setting out to make everything better with Go, we had made JavaScript better as well. I consider this an excellent outcome. 😃

And then the whole server wanted to leave

By this point, turning one ABAP report into a native program worked. But Open SteamGate already contained a substantial collection of ABAP classes, including its Gateway and the services behind the demo applications, so the next question was whether we could compile those too.

That is how OSGo happened. Instead of building one report with a small runtime closure, OSGo compiles the supported part of Open SteamGate's application-server runtime to Go: one native executable with the compiled ABAP services and their initial data, and SQLite through a Go driver. Start the binary, and it serves actual OData requests, with no JavaScript server process and no separate database server in that configuration. It doesn't yet provide every feature of the Node-based OSG host — in particular, it doesn't serve the ADT façade — but running the OData side as one executable was already a substantial milestone.

OSGo: the whole server as one Go binary.
 
A real OData request and its JSON answer.

There is something pleasing about compiling an application-server implementation written in ABAP into a Go executable and then using that executable to serve ABAP applications. It is a little recursive, but we seem to be getting used to that.

The report compiler gives us another practical possibility: ABAP programs that are useful without behaving like application servers at all. A report that transforms files, analyses data or runs a batch operation can become a native command with its own SQLite database, taking its arguments from a script or asking for them in the terminal, and the ABAP doesn't have to be rewritten just because its destination has changed. Once the compiler knows enough about a program, the place where it runs becomes a design choice rather than an assumption built into the language.

Of course, someone may reasonably ask whether this means my ABAP can run on a ZX Spectrum as well.

 
ZX Spectrum: FLEET.bin · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80 · sha256 2d52a6a2…dc74 · real capture, 10 s of emulated time, original 352×304 frames, no crop, scaling or compositing; not a benchmark. MZX emulator, Pentagon 128 model; the TR-DOS disk image is read through sector traps, no system or DOS ROM executed; no physical-hardware claim. The same 1,875-byte ABAP source as below. minz PR #203, merged.
 
 
CP/M: FLEET.COM · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80 · real capture, unmodified frames, about 8 s; Z80/MZE CP/M emulation, no physical-hardware claim. The same 1,875-byte ABAP report: F4 → FLEET.CSV → GUI_UPLOAD → typed table → cl_salv_table.
 
Agon: FLEET.BIN · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80-mode code on eZ80 · real capture, unmodified frames, real debugger pauses, not a benchmark. Both MinZ PRs are merged (#200, #201).

AgonLight2 (powered by eZ80) is quite a remarkable computer, by the way: AgonLight2 - Open Source Hardware Board

It can, a little. That is a different compiler, MinZ, with a rather smaller processor and its own adventures, including the occasional emulator that starts quite happily and then declines to execute the program we gave it. We'll get back to that one; I still have a terminal to show you.

Try letting your ABAP out

If you want to play with this, start with the examples under gogen in Open SteamGate. Building the native executables needs the development toolchain, including Go 1.26, but the resulting binaries can be copied and run on their target platform on their own. In a checkout, osd run compiles and runs a report in one step, and F8 on a report in VS Code does the same.

For an application-sized example, osg-demo has a chapter called My ABAP Escaped from the Server, which follows an airship-fleet report as its selection screen becomes a terminal form, its parameters become command-line options, and its local tables become a SQLite database. The fleet has been remarkably patient with this project, and I am beginning to suspect that the Old Boiler is less an airship and more an integration-test platform.

And I particularly recommend the file-selection example, zpickfile, because pressing F4 on a native command-line program generated from ABAP is something I still find entertaining.

And one more: F4 picks a CSV, cl_gui_frontend_services=>gui_upload reads it, and the report lists it with the headings from its first line.

BTW, does it look like R/2?

If you manage to break it, I'd genuinely like to know how. There are plenty of ABAP constructs and runtime behaviours still to implement, and a small report that behaves differently on SAP and on the native runtime is exactly what helps an independent implementation improve.

I started by wanting to run ABAP outside SAP, then without a server, and then I wanted the report's selection screen back. Along the way we ended up with a typed representation of ABAP, two code-generation backends, a faster JavaScript path and a Go application-server runtime — quite a journey for a report that only wanted to print a few lines. I still like JavaScript, I still like Go, and I now have ABAP programs that can travel between them, which is quite a nice place to be.

Except that, somewhere around the same time, I started working on another question. If we can compile ABAP into JavaScript and Go, what happens if we turn the whole arrangement around, take code written in TypeScript, and compile it into ABAP? And perhaps take an entire tool such as abaplint, written in TypeScript, and run it inside the very ABAP system whose code it was created to inspect?

It was not the first idea. Lars and I had been circling this question for a while, independently and not quite independently, each borrowing the other’s successes and failures in roughly equal measure. Lars went first with abap-wasm, a WebAssembly virtual machine written in ABAP: nearly everything compiles to WASM these days, so an interpreter for it on the stack opens a large door at once. I had spent some time on interpreters of my own by then — zork-abap runs Infocom’s Z-machine on SAP, cpm-abap is a Z80/i8080 emulator that runs CP/M programs, and there was a 6502 as well — so I thought a WASM compiler, rather than an interpreter, might be the more promising route. It turned out that WASM sits at too low a level of abstraction for the lift back to ABAP: you get a stack machine and a linear memory, and everything that would make the output readable has already been compiled away.

interpreting twice is interpreting too often - the fifth approach moves the work into a compiler

So I tried from the other end, with a JavaScript interpreter, which became ZMJS, a mini JavaScript engine in about two thousand lines of ABAP. It runs on a real system and even runs the abaplint lexer there. Lars then did the serious version, ZQJS, a port of Fabrice Bellard’s QuickJS engine to ABAP, which is a far more complete JavaScript. Both work. Both were too slow for the practical target, which was running abaplint itself on the stack, in a time a developer would wait for; an interpreter written in an interpreted language is interpreting twice, and that is at least once too often.

What I had left was the MinZ frontend. MinZ already lowers several languages — Nanz, MinZ, Lizp, Lanz, ABAP, PL/M, Pascal — into one high-level intermediate representation, HIR, before any of them goes anywhere near a Z80. So what if TypeScript and JavaScript were lowered into that same HIR, and then lifted back out as idiomatic ABAP? Classes, functions, closures and interfaces look remarkably alike across modern languages; the real differences are small and nameable, the main one being that JavaScript treats arrays as references while ABAP treats internal tables as values. Differences of that kind can be handled as explicit edge cases, and the rewrites that handle them are stated once in Grace, an S-expression language for rewriting and optimisation, rather than scattered through a code generator. That is ABAPiti, and it is where abaplint, written in TypeScript, comes back to the stack as ABAP.

Well. It seems ABAP was leaving the application server just as TypeScript was arriving.

They must have passed each other on the way. 😃

Next time: ABAPiti — A Journey Towards Self-Hosting.

entry.title: #Demystifying AI Series — Episode 1 #SAP Is Going AI-First. Here's What That Actually Means for You.
entry.content:
DEMYSTIFYING AI SERIES  ·  EPISODE 01 

SAP Is Going AI-First.

Here's What That Actually Means for You.

 

💡  SAP just declared AI its number one priority. But what does "AI-First" mean when you're the one sitting in front of the system every day?

 

The Memo Nobody Sent You

One day, you're configuring a purchase order in S/4HANA.

The next day, there's a little "Ask Joule" button in the corner of your screen.

Nobody called a meeting. Nobody sent you a roadmap. The software just... changed.

That's what "AI-First" actually looks like on the ground.

SAP didn't announce "AI-First, Suite-First" in a press release for fun. This is the defining strategy for everything they build, sell, and invest in — from now through 2026 and beyond. Over 400 embedded AI use cases are live or in flight by end of 2025, across finance, supply chain, HR, procurement, and more.

Not as add-ons. Embedded. In the core.

And if you're an SAP professional, that changes things — whether you're ready for it or not.

So What Does "AI-First" Actually Mean?

Let me break it down without the buzzwords.

"AI-First" means that when SAP's engineers design a new feature — any feature — AI isn't an afterthought. It's built in from day one. The system learns from your data. It suggests. It predicts. It acts.

"Suite-First" means all of this is connected. Joule, SAP's AI copilot, doesn't live in just one product. It moves with you across S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba, and more. One interface. One context. Your business data flowing through it all.

And here's the number that stopped me when I first saw it: in 2024, 7% of companies were using AI as an integral part of their processes. By end of 2025, that number is 29% — and another 51% are actively adopting AI on a project basis.

The shift is already happening. The question is where you are in it.

The Three Things AI Actually Does to Your Work

I keep coming back to three words SAP uses to describe AI's impact on business.

Accelerate —  AI shortens the gap between having a question and getting an answer. You ask in natural language, you get a result. You stop digging through five menu paths for a number that should take five seconds.

Augment —  AI gives you capabilities you didn't have before. Not replacing you — giving you superpowers. Predictive demand forecasting that used to require a data science team. Anomaly detection that surfaces problems before they become incidents.

Automate —  The long tail of repetitive tasks starts running without you. Invoice reconciliation. Approval routing. Periodic reports nobody loved writing anyway.

❓  Now here's the question nobody asks: which of these three is happening to your specific job right now?
That answer will shape your next two years more than any certification.

Meet the Thing Living Inside Your SAP System

You've probably heard of Joule. Maybe you rolled your eyes a little.

Fair. There have been a lot of "AI assistants" that turned out to be glorified search bars.

Joule is different — not because of the marketing, but because of the architecture.

By end of 2025, SAP has 40 Joule Agents running across its portfolio, built on over 2,100 Joule Skills. Not just Joule answering questions. Joule doing things — executing workflows, completing tasks, operating with a level of autonomy that's genuinely new territory for enterprise software.

All of this runs on SAP AI Foundation on BTP — the platform SAP calls the "AI operating system" for its entire Business AI portfolio. And underneath that sits Business Data Cloud — a unified, governed data layer that connects SAP and non-SAP data so the AI isn't guessing. It knows your processes. Your history. Your context.

When SAP says "relevant, reliable, responsible AI" — this is what makes it relevant. It's grounded in your actual business data, not a generic model of the world.

What This Means If You're an SAP Professional Today

I'll be straight with you.

If your daily work is mostly repetitive execution — running standard reports, processing standard transactions, following standard procedures — AI is coming for that work. Not to fire you. To do those parts faster, so you can do something else.

The question is: what is that something else?

The SAP professionals I see positioning themselves well right now are the ones shifting from executing the system to shaping the system. They understand what Joule can do. They know where AI recommendations need human judgment. They're the ones who can look at an AI output and say "that's right" or "that's wrong" — and explain why.

That ability to critically evaluate AI in a real business context? Joule can't do that for you. That's yours.

The Autonomous Enterprise Is the Destination — We're in the Messy Middle

SAP calls it the Autonomous Enterprise — a future where processes self-optimize, decisions happen faster, and humans focus on what genuinely requires human thinking.

We're not there yet. We're in the messy middle.

AI is everywhere but uneven. Powerful but imperfect. Exciting and, if I'm honest, a little disorienting at times.

That's exactly why now is the right time to start paying attention — not to become an AI expert, but to become the SAP professional who understands what AI can and can't do, and uses that knowledge to work differently.

That's what this series is about. One episode at a time, we'll demystify what AI actually means in the SAP world. Not hype. Not fear. Just an honest look at what's changing, what it means for your work, and what to do about it.

 

Your Turn

Which part of your SAP work do you think will be most affected by AI in the next 12 months? Drop a comment — I'm genuinely curious what you're seeing from your corner of the ecosystem.

⏭  Next episode: Meet Joule — and why calling it a "chatbot" completely misses the point.

entry.title: Part 1: From OData to MCP: Building an MCP Server with SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Hi everyone!

Recently, I’ve been experimenting with MCP on SAP Integration Suite and looking at a practical question:

What does it actually take to make an existing enterprise API consumable by an AI client through MCP?

Rather than building an AI-specific backend, I wanted to start with something we already know well: an existing OData API.

For this experiment, I used the Business Partner (A2X) API from SAP Business Accelerator Hub and exposed selected capabilities through an MCP Server running on SAP Integration Suite’s Integration Cell runtime.

In this first part, we’ll build the provider side of the scenario:

Business Partner OData API → SAP Integration Suite / Integration Cell → MCP Server → Developer Hub

By the end of this article, we’ll have an MCP capability deployed on Integration Cell, published through Developer Hub, and ready for an MCP client to consume.

The underlying idea is important: we are not replacing the existing OData API or building a special AI backend. We are making an existing enterprise capability available to a new type of consumer through MCP.

In Part 2, we’ll take the next step: connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client and see what happens when the user stops thinking about OData endpoints, entities, filters, and query syntax, and simply expresses what they want in natural language.

 

 

Step-by-Step: From Business Partner OData API to MCP

Step 0: What we are building

In Part 1, we are building the provider side of the end-to-end scenario.

We’ll start with the existing Business Partner (A2X) OData API, bring it into SAP Integration Suite as an API artifact, expose selected capabilities through an MCP Server running on Integration Cell, and finally publish that MCP Server through Developer Hub.

The flow we’ll build is:

Business Partner (A2X) API
↓ OData
SAP Integration Suite / Integration Cell
↓
MCP Server
↓
Developer Hub / Product / Subscription

By the end of Part 1, the enterprise capability will be ready for an MCP client to consume.

For more background on MCP in SAP Integration Suite, see the SAP Integration Suite MCP Server documentation.

Step 1: Check the prerequisites

Before we start, make sure your SAP Integration Suite environment is ready.

For this scenario, you will need:

  • SAP Integration Suite with API Management activated
  • An active Integration Cell runtime
  • The appropriate Cloud Integration and API Management roles
  • Access to Developer Hub
  • An API that we can expose through MCP

Don't have an SAP BTP environment?

The good news is that you can also experiment with this scenario using an SAP BTP Trial account.

If you don't already have one, follow the SAP Developer tutorial Get an Account on SAP BTP Trial to set up your trial environment.

Once your SAP BTP Trial account is ready, you can continue with the SAP Integration Suite and Integration Cell setup required for this scenario.

The current SAP hands-on MCP Gateway tutorial also uses an SAP BTP Trial account as a prerequisite, so this is a convenient way to reproduce the scenario without requiring an existing productive SAP BTP landscape.

The MCP Server artifact is currently listed as available with Enhanced, Premium, Trial, and Free Tier SAP Integration Suite service plans. See Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

 
This means you don't necessarily need an existing productive SAP Integration Suite landscape to start experimenting with MCP.

Checkpoint

Before continuing, verify that:

✓ SAP Integration Suite is available
✓ API Management is activated
✓ Integration Cell is active
✓ You have access to Developer Hub
✓ You have an API to use for this exercise

Step 2: Find the Business Partner (A2X) API

For this demo, I wanted to start with an existing SAP business API rather than create a backend specifically for MCP.

A convenient place to explore available SAP APIs is SAP Business Accelerator Hub. The catalogue contains thousands of APIs, so it is worth being precise about which one I used for this scenario.

For this tutorial, I used:

Business Partner (A2X)
API identifier: API_BUSINESS_PARTNER

This is important because searching for “Business Partner” in SAP Business Accelerator Hub returns multiple Business Partner-related APIs and resources. To reproduce this scenario, make sure you are working with the Business Partner (A2X) API rather than another Business Partner integration.

Once you have opened the API, take a few minutes to explore its available resources and operations. For this demo, I'm interested in capabilities that support the following progression:

  1. Find Business Partners.
  2. Retrieve more information about a selected Business Partner.
  3. Present that information to the user in a useful way.

At this point, there is nothing MCP-specific about the backend. We're simply identifying the existing business capability that we eventually want our AI client to consume.

Later, when an MCP client consumes this capability, the underlying business information will still come from this existing enterprise API.

Why this matters

We're not designing an API specifically for an AI client. We're taking a business capability that already exists and introducing a new way to consume it.

Step 3: Make the API available as an API artifact on Integration Cell

Now that we have identified the API we want to expose, let's bring it into SAP Integration Suite.

Navigate to:

Integration Suite → Design → Integrations and APIs → Integration Package → Edit → Artifacts → Add → API

For details on creating API artifacts, see Create a Reusable API Artifact.

For our scenario, the result looks conceptually like this:

Business Partner API
        │
      OData
        ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite     │
│                           │
│ API artifact              │
│ Integration Cell runtime  │
└───────────────────────────┘

 

Configure backend authentication

There is one important detail in my setup.

The Business Partner API used as the backend requires an API key. Therefore, the request from the API artifact to the backend also needs to carry the appropriate backend credential.

I configured the API key on the API artifact/policy side so that the MCP consumer does not need to know or provide the backend credential.

This introduces an important distinction that we will see again later:

SAP Integration Suite
     │
     │ Backend authentication / API key
     ▼
Business Partner API
The credential used by the MCP client to access the MCP Server and the credential used by SAP Integration Suite to access the backend API serve different purposes.

Checkpoint

Before adding MCP to the picture, verify that the API artifact can successfully access the backend.

I found this separation very useful while building the demo. If the API layer works independently, any problem introduced afterwards is much easier to isolate.

Step 4: Create the MCP Server

Now we can put the MCP layer in front of the API.

In SAP Integration Suite, navigate to:

Design → Integrations and APIs → Integration Package → Artifacts → Add → MCP Server

Select the appropriate API as the source for the MCP Server.

You can find a complete example in Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

At this point, the architecture starts to look like this:

MCP Client
     │
     │ MCP
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ MCP Server              │
│                         │
│ Integration Cell        │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │
             │ OData
             ▼
    Business Partner API
 
This is where the existing API capability starts becoming consumable through an AI-oriented interface.

Step 5: Decide what to expose through MCP

This is an important design point.

Rather than asking:

How many API operations can I expose?

I prefer to start with:

What capabilities does my MCP client actually need?

For this demo, we can work backwards from the desired conversation:

"Find business partners..."
           ↓
Need Business Partner search/retrieval

"Tell me more about the first one..."
           ↓
Need additional Business Partner details

This keeps the MCP capabilities closely aligned with the actual user scenario.

The underlying API still provides the business functions. MCP introduces a way for an AI client to discover and invoke the capabilities we choose to expose.

For additional background, see the MCP Server documentation.

Step 6: Review the MCP policy model

Before deploying the MCP Server, let's take a look at the policy model.

This is an important part of the architecture because the MCP Server doesn't simply expose the backend API directly to the AI client. The MCP request is handled through SAP Integration Suite, giving us a managed layer between the MCP consumer and the enterprise service.

For this demo, I kept the default policy model and reviewed the authentication and authorization configuration before deployment.

Conceptually, we now have:

    MCP Client
        │
       MCP
        ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite    │
│                          │
│ MCP Gateway / Policies   │
│ MCP Server               │
└────────────┬─────────────┘
             │
           OData
             ▼
    Business Partner API

The important point is that the AI client does not connect directly to the Business Partner API. SAP Integration Suite sits between the MCP consumer and the underlying enterprise capability.

Two authentication contexts

At this stage it is useful to keep the two security contexts separate:

MCP Client 
 │
 │ MCP client authentication
 │
 ▼
SAP Integration Suite
 │
 │ Backend authentication / API key
 │
 ▼
Business Partner API
We will come back to the client side of this authentication model in Part 2, when we connect Joule Work Desktop to the capability exposed here.

Step 7: Deploy the MCP Server

Now deploy the MCP Server to the Integration Cell runtime.

The server side of our architecture is now essentially complete:

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite      │
│                            │
│ Integration Cell Runtime   │
│                            │
│      MCP Server            │
└──────────────┬─────────────┘
               │
             OData
               ▼
       Business Partner API

The SAP tutorial Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents also walks through deploying an MCP Server to Integration Cell.

Checkpoint

Before moving on, confirm that the MCP Server has been deployed successfully.

Now we have the runtime capability. The next question is how our MCP client discovers and consumes it.

Step 8: Publish the MCP Server through Developer Hub

How do I access Developer Hub?

Developer Hub is part of the API Management capabilities in SAP Integration Suite. If you haven't activated it yet, enable Developer Hub in your Integration Suite capabilities first.

Once it is activated, open the product switcher in the SAP Integration Suite header and select Developer Hub.

If you're setting this up for the first time, check the required role collections as well. For the complete setup, see Activating Developer Hub.

This was one of the most important discoveries in my own JWD test.

Once the MCP Server was running on Integration Cell, I published it through Developer Hub as part of a product.

The consumption flow becomes:

Integration Suite
      │
 MCP Server
      │
      ▼
Developer Hub
      │
   Product
      │
      ▼
MCP Consumer

In Developer Hub:

  1. Open Admin Center → Manage Content.
  2. Select the Integration Suite business system.
  3. Open the MCP Servers tab.
  4. Select the MCP Server created earlier.
  5. Choose Create Product.
  6. Provide the product name, ID, and description.
  7. Confirm that the correct MCP Server is included.
  8. Publish the product.

For the detailed publishing flow, see Discover and Publish MCP Servers from SAP Integration Suite.

For me, this step was the bridge between “I have an MCP Server running” and “I have an MCP capability that my client can actually consume.”

Step 9: Subscribe to the product

Once the product is published, subscribe to it through Developer Hub.

The end-to-end consumption flow is:

Publish MCP Server
        ↓
Publish Product
        ↓
Subscribe to Product
        ↓
Retrieve Credentials
        ↓
Configure MCP Client

This sequence turned out to be particularly important in my JWD setup.

At this point, Developer Hub is doing more than simply making the MCP Server visible. The subscription gives us the consumption information needed for the client connection.

For another end-to-end example of this flow, see Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

Step 10: Retrieve the client credentials

After subscribing to the product, retrieve the OAuth credentials needed by the MCP consumer.

And this is where I learned something useful.

Lesson learned from my first attempt

Initially, I tried creating credentials manually through a Process Integration Runtime Service Key.

That turned out not to be the path I needed for this scenario.

Once I published the MCP Server through Developer Hub, subscribed to the product, and used the credentials obtained through that consumption flow, the JWD connection worked.

There's also an important point in the current product documentation: the Process Integration Runtime credential approach is described as an anti-pattern, with credentials obtained through Developer Hub strongly recommended instead.

See Invoke an MCP Server Artifact by Obtaining Credentials through Process Integration Runtime.

So my practical takeaway is:

For this scenario, use the Developer Hub publication, subscription, and credential flow for the MCP client rather than starting with a manually created Process Integration Runtime Service Key.

What we have built

At this point, we have completed the provider side of the scenario:

Business Partner API → API artifact → MCP Server → Integration Cell → Developer Hub → Subscription

The existing Business Partner API remains responsible for the underlying business capability. SAP Integration Suite provides the layer through which selected capabilities are exposed via MCP, while Developer Hub provides the consumption path we will use for the MCP client.

But so far, we have only built the provider side.

The more interesting question is what happens when an AI client starts consuming that capability.

Coming next: From MCP to Natural Language

In Part 2, I'll connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client and move away from API terminology entirely.

Instead of thinking about endpoints or query parameters, we'll ask:

“Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.”

Then we'll continue the same conversation:

“Tell me more about the first one, including its address and contact information.”

And finally:

“Summarize what we know about this business partner in a way that would be useful before a customer call.”

That's where this experiment becomes much more interesting.

entry.title: Part 2: From MCP to Natural Language: SAP Integration Suite and Joule Work Desktop
entry.content:
Hi everyone, and welcome to Part 2!

In Part 1, we started with an existing Business Partner (A2X) OData API, brought it into SAP Integration Suite as an API artifact, exposed selected capabilities through an MCP Server on Integration Cell, and published the result through Developer Hub.

Now comes the part that originally made this experiment interesting to me.

What happens when the user stops thinking about APIs and simply expresses what they want in natural language?

Our complete architecture now looks like this:

Let's connect JWD and try it.

 

 

Step 1: Connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client

 
If you haven't completed the MCP Server and Developer Hub setup yet, start with Part 1: From OData to MCP.

Now we can finally connect the client.

For this demo, I used Joule Work Desktop (JWD) as the MCP client and configured the connection using the MCP endpoint and OAuth information obtained through Developer Hub.

Conceptually, we have now completed the entire architecture:

Joule Work Desktop
        │
       MCP
        ▼
SAP Integration Suite
        │
   MCP Server
        │
Integration Cell Runtime
        │
      OData
        ▼
Business Partner API

Once the connector appeared as available in JWD, the configuration was behind us and I was ready to test the complete flow from the user's perspective using natural language.

This is where things become much more interesting.

Step 2: Ask the first natural-language question

Now comes the fun part.

The prompts in this example are intentionally simple.

I'm not trying to demonstrate advanced prompt engineering or prescribe a specific output format. Instead, I want to see how naturally a user can express an intent when the underlying enterprise capability is exposed through MCP.

In a production scenario, prompts could certainly be more explicit about scope, output format, constraints, and expected behaviour. For this experiment, however, I've deliberately kept them conversational.

Instead of testing the integration using API terminology, I ask JWD:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

What's interesting is what I didn't have to specify:

  • an OData endpoint;
  • an entity name;
  • query parameters;
  • filter syntax; or
  • a response structure.

I simply described what I wanted.

That is a very different consumption experience from working directly with an API.

But underneath that simple sentence, we are still using the Business Partner capability that we started with in Part 1.

Step 3: Continue the same conversation

The next test is deliberately not another independent API request.

I simply continue:

Tell me more about the first one, including its address and contact information.

The interesting phrase here is:

“the first one”

From the user's perspective, this is a continuation of the conversation.

There is no need to copy a Business Partner identifier from one result, work out another API operation, and construct another technical request.

The user simply expresses the next intent in the conversation.

Step 4: Move from data retrieval to business intent

Finally, I take it one step further:

Summarize what we know about this business partner in a way that would be useful before a customer call.

The progression now looks like this:

1. Find enterprise data
             │
             ▼
2. Continue conversationally
             │
             ▼
3. Turn the retrieved information
   into a user-oriented response

This is the point where, for me, the scenario becomes more interesting than simply saying “an LLM can call an API.”

We're starting with existing enterprise capabilities and changing how a user can interact with them.

Step 5: What just happened?

 
Let's return to the architecture one more time:

And this brings us back to the main point of the experiment:

The Business Partner API didn't have to become conversational.

It remains an enterprise API.

The MCP Server makes selected capabilities available through MCP, while SAP Integration Suite provides the runtime layer between the MCP consumer and the underlying enterprise service.

You can find more detail about this architecture in the SAP Integration Suite MCP documentation.

What I learned

A few things stood out to me while putting this scenario together.

1. Existing APIs become more valuable, not less

MCP doesn't mean replacing our existing REST or OData APIs.

In this scenario, the Business Partner API remains the underlying business capability. What changes is the way that capability can be exposed and consumed.

That gives our existing API investments another potential class of consumer: AI clients and agents.

2. The user experience changes dramatically

Compare the traditional API consumption process:

 
Understand the API
        ↓
Understand the data model
        ↓
Construct the request
        ↓
Process the response

with:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

The underlying business capability can remain the same while the consumer experience becomes completely different.

3. MCP authentication and backend authentication are different concerns

This became especially clear while building the demo.

On one side, JWD authenticates as an MCP consumer.

On the other side, Integration Suite has to authenticate when invoking the backend Business Partner API.

 
JWD
 │
 │ MCP authentication
 ▼
SAP Integration Suite
 │
 │ Backend authentication
 ▼
Business Partner API

Keeping these two concerns separate made the architecture, and the troubleshooting, much clearer.

4. Developer Hub was the missing piece for my JWD connection

My initial attempt focused too much on creating credentials directly.

The successful path was:

Deploy → Publish through Developer Hub → Subscribe → Retrieve credentials → Connect JWD

Once I followed that consumption model, the pieces came together.

Closing thoughts

For me, this is where MCP starts to get really interesting.

The exciting part isn't that an AI client can execute an HTTP request. It's that we can take business capabilities that already exist, selectively expose them through MCP, and let users interact with those capabilities in terms of intent rather than API implementation.

The Business Partner API remains an API.

What changed is how the capability is discovered, invoked, and experienced by the user.

And that raises an interesting question for integration architects:

As AI clients become another consumer of enterprise capabilities, how should we design, expose, secure, and govern the APIs behind them?

I'd love to hear how others are exploring MCP in their own integration scenarios. If you've tried connecting MCP clients to SAP Integration Suite, or have a different approach to exposing enterprise APIs to AI clients, please share your experience, questions, or lessons learned in the comments below. Let's learn from each other!

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) in SAP Integration Suite
  • Build and Govern MCP Servers with SAP Integration Suite
  • Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents
  • Create a Reusable API Artifact
  • Discover and Publish MCP Servers from SAP Integration Suite
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub

entry.title: How to Reverse or Correct Wrongly Migrated Data in Asset Accounting
entry.content:
Option 1 — Reverse the Transfer Posting (All Systems — Q & P)

When to use: Incorrect takeover values were posted, but no depreciation has been posted yet (or follow-on postings can be reversed).

How it works: SAP posts a journal entry when asset values are transferred via Migration Cockpit. This document can be reversed in Manage Fixed Assets app.

If wrong transfer values were posted, you must reverse the journal entry and then enter the transfer values again.

You can only change transfer values by reversing the posted transfer document and making a new posting. To be able to reverse a transfer document, subsequent transactions are not allowed to exist on the fixed asset.

If follow-on transactions were already posted on the fixed asset, we recommend you proceed as follows:

  1. Reverse all transactions in reverse chronological order.

  2. Reverse the transfer transaction.

  3. Post the new transfer values.

  4. Enter the follow-on transactions again individually.

Option 2 — Reset Transaction Data (Q System / Test System Only)

When to use: Large volumes of incorrect data were migrated to the Q/Test system and a full cleanup is needed before re-migration.

⚠️ This option is NOT available in Production (P system). It will delete broad financial data across the company code.

If you have transferred legacy data with errors to the Q system, either manually or using the SAP S/4HANA migration cockpit, you can completely delete this incorrect data.

To do so, use the Reset Transaction Data job template from the app Schedule Accounting Data Changes.

You use this job template to delete master data and transaction data from Asset Accounting, along with other accounting data.

Note

It is not possible to only delete the Asset Accounting data and keep the other data of the company code. This would lead to inconsistencies because Asset Accounting is highly integrated with other application components such as General Ledger Accounting and the Controlling components.

Note

You can only use the job template in the quality management system (Q system), and not in the production system (P system).

entry.title: Re: I counted the released APIs in my S/4HANA 2023 lab. The BAPI numbers surprised me
entry.content:
@Jelena_Perfiljeva "Same problems, new Cloud" made me laugh. Then I went to check before answering.

The "no documentation" part is true, at least inside the system. I looked for the classic documentation of the CL_BALI / IF_BALI objects in S/4HANA 2020, 2023 and 2025. Zero in all three. The family grew from 29 released objects in 2020 to 31 in 2023 (the item filter came in) and stayed at 31 in 2025, and none of them ever got a line of documentation in the system. CL_ABAP_TYPEDESCR has class and method docs in the same three systems, so it's not my query. What exists is on SAP Help.

For your log_this_stuff( my_stuff ), the closest thing I found is not BALI, it's XCO_CP_BAL. It is released for ABAP Cloud (C1) in the same three releases and on BTP:

DATA(log) = xco_cp_bal=>for->database( )->log->create( iv_object = 'ZMY_LOG' iv_subobject = 'ZMY_SUB' iv_external_id = 'whatever' ).

log->add_text( xco_cp=>string( my_stuff ) ).

And that's it, there is no save call. With the database persistence, every item you add is saved and committed on a secondary database connection. I read it in the code: XCO_CP_BAL=>FOR->DATABASE( ) creates the persistence with both "second connection" flags set to abap_true, and its FLUSH calls BAL_DB_SAVE with them. The SAP Help page of the XCO BAL module says the same. With CL_BALI_LOG the same result goes through CL_BALI_HEADER_SETTER, CL_BALI_FREE_TEXT_SETTER and CL_BALI_LOG_DB->SAVE_LOG at the end.

add_message( ) takes a SYMSG, and add_exception( ) takes any CX_ROOT and, with the standard profile, also logs the previous exceptions.

It's still not one line. You need the log object (APLO) created first. But it's two lines instead of a ceremony.

I only did a syntax check of this on the BTP ABAP environment (plus a misspelled method as a negative control, which failed as expected). I didn't run it, and I didn't measure what one commit per item costs inside a big loop. If you or someone did, I'd like to know.

entry.title: Re: Report sending email with PDF attached containing ALV with hierarchy format
entry.content:
@jeff_broodwar yes, I tested exactly that in my lab, and you don't need REUSE_ALV_FIELDCATALOG_MERGE at all.

You already have the LVC field catalogs of your two grids (LVC_T_FCAT). Function module LVC_TRANSFER_TO_SLIS converts each one, and the layout too, to the SLIS format the block list wants. So the offline branch reuses the same catalogs you pass to SET_TABLE_FOR_FIRST_DISPLAY:

IF cl_gui_alv_grid=>offline( ) = 1.   " job or print, no GUI
  CALL FUNCTION 'LVC_TRANSFER_TO_SLIS'
    EXPORTING it_fieldcat_lvc = lt_fcat1        " the catalog of grid 1
              is_layout_lvc   = ls_layout1
    IMPORTING et_fieldcat_alv = lt_slis1
              es_layout_alv   = ls_slis_layout1
    TABLES    it_data         = gt_tab1
    EXCEPTIONS OTHERS         = 1.
  " the same for grid 2
  CALL FUNCTION 'REUSE_ALV_BLOCK_LIST_INIT'
    EXPORTING i_callback_program = sy-repid.
  CALL FUNCTION 'REUSE_ALV_BLOCK_LIST_APPEND'
    EXPORTING is_layout = ls_slis_layout1  it_fieldcat = lt_slis1
              i_tabname = 'GT_TAB1'        it_events   = lt_events
    TABLES    t_outtab  = gt_tab1.
  " the same APPEND for the second table
  CALL FUNCTION 'REUSE_ALV_BLOCK_LIST_DISPLAY'
    EXPORTING is_print = VALUE slis_print_alv( no_print_listinfos = 'X' ).
ELSE.
  " your splitter with the two grids, as today
ENDIF.

What I ran, in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, as a background job and with SUBMIT ... TO SAP-SPOOL: grid 1 with a catalog from LVC_FIELDCATALOG_MERGE (80 rows), and grid 2 with a local type and a catalog built by hand, where one column has no DDIC reference at all, only COLTEXT (20 rows). Both converted, the hand-made column printed with its header, and both tables came out in one spool request.

Two small things I found on the way:

  • NO_PRINT_LISTINFOS = 'X' in IS_PRINT removes the small statistics box the block list prints for each table. My spool went from 5 pages to 3.
  • IT_DATA looked mandatory when I read the code (LVC_TRANSFER_TO_KKBLO, called inside, has a RAISE it_data_missing), so I tested without it too: same catalog, sy-subrc 0. That RAISE only fires when IT_DATA is not requested, and LVC_TRANSFER_TO_SLIS always passes its own IT_DATA down. I still pass it, it costs nothing.

The spool number and the PDF are the same as in my previous answer (the newest TSP01 entry of the user, and PDF_DESTINATION = 'X'). LVC_TRANSFER_TO_SLIS is also there in my S/4HANA 2020 and 2025 systems, same function group, so the release shouldn't matter.

What I didn't test: sorts and filters (LVC_TRANSFER_TO_SLIS also takes IT_SORT_LVC and IT_FILTER_LVC), and screen-only settings like hotspots or toolbar buttons.

entry.title: I taught SAP RPT-1.6 to play Tetris
entry.content:
Video: SAP RPT-1.6 playing live through SAP AI Core. Unedited real-time screen recording (seconds 6–16 of a game, seed 1). Every piece you see was placed by one RPT prediction request. On the right, the "Last decision" table shows RPT's score for each candidate next to the heuristic value it learned from.

SAP RPT-1.6 is a tabular foundation model. It does not chat and it does not generate text. You give it a table in which some cel [PREDICT], and it fills them in, using the other rows of the same table as examples. That is all it does.

Inspired by the LinkedIn post of Philipp Herzig showing RPT 1.6 playing Snake against Jev,  I asked a playful question: can a model that only knows how to complete tables play Tetris? Not with a Tetris model trained for weeks, but with the stock model on SAP AI Core, the same model you would use to predict delivery delays or payment dates.

It can. Over two 100-piece games, RPT-1.6 cleared 38 and 35 lines. The hand-tuned heuristic it learned from cleared 38 and 39. No weights were changed. Everything RPT knows about Tetris arrives in the request, as 64 example rows per move.

This post explains how that works: how a game move becomes a table, what goes into the context, and why a table model can make good moves at all.

Step 1: Turn a move into a table

Tetris looks like a vision or reinforcement-learning problem. The trick is to stop thinking about pixels and key presses and think about options.

When a piece appears, there is only a small, finite set of places it can end up: every combination of rotation and column the piece can actually reach. For a T piece that's 34 placements, for an O piece 9. My game engine lists all of them, including the moves that need wall kicks.

For each placement, the engine simulates the drop and describes the board after the move. That description is one table row.

Figure 1: A real position from my game (move 19, falling T, next piece I). Each legal placement becomes one row whose features describe the board after that placement. The outcome column is the one RPT has to fill in.

The columns fall into four groups:

Group Columns Meaning
What is placedpiece, next_piece, rotation, columnthe piece, the preview piece, and the pose
What it doeslines_cleared, eroded_cells, holes, holes_delta, landing_heightimmediate consequences of the move
Shape of the board afteragg_height, max_height, bumpiness, row_transitions, col_transitions, wells, levelhow healthy the stack is afterwards
Labeloutcomehow good this move is: known for examples, [PREDICT] for candidates

A row_id column (for example demo:19:1:3 = game, move, rotation, column) is sent as RPT's index_column, so every prediction comes back with the ID of its row. I can also send the ten column heights h0–h9 (28 columns in total). By default I leave them out and use 18 columns, which keeps requests smaller and faster.

With this framing, "play Tetris" turns into "which row has the best outcome?". That is a question a table model can answer.

Step 2: Teach with context rows, not with training

RPT has never seen Tetris. It learns what a good move looks like from context rows: rows like the candidates above, but with outcome filled in.

Figure 2: One request is one table. 64 labeled example rows (blue) teach the task; the 34 candidates of the current piece (orange) carry [PREDICT]. RPT-1.6 returns a predicted outcome per row, and the game plays the best one. The numbers are from a real call.

Where do the labels come from? I used a teacher: the well-known El-Tetris heuristic, a hand-tuned formula that weighs six board features (landing height, eroded cells, row and column transitions, holes, wells). When the server starts:

  1. It simulates 30 games with the heuristic. In a third of the games it follows the heuristic exactly; in the others it makes 15% or 40% random moves, so the examples also include messy, high stacks and bad situations.
  2. For every move of those games it labels every candidate, good and bad, with the heuristic score. The examples show the whole range from "great move" to "terrible move", not just the winners.
  3. These 5,000 labeled rows go into an experience store.

For every move in the live game, the server samples 64 rows from that store. Roughly 70% come from situations with a similar stack height (±3 rows), the rest at random. Those 64 rows plus the current candidates form one request: for a T piece 64 + 34 = 98 rows × 18 columns, roughly 1,800 cells.

One detail matters for understanding the result: the heuristic formula is never sent to RPT. RPT sees only rows and numbers. It has to work out from 64 examples that holes are bad and cleared lines are good, and by how much.

Step 3: Why a table model can play Tetris at all

Figure 3: Classic ML trains and deploys a dedicated model per task. With RPT-1.6, the training step is replaced by labeled rows inside each request, sent to a frozen, pretrained model.

The model is not "playing" in the sense a human does. It never sees the board and has no notion of falling blocks. Three things make it work anyway.

1. The features carry the game knowledge. Each row already encodes the consequences of a move. Choosing the best placement turns into ranking rows, and ranking rows by a predicted number is plain regression, the bread and butter of a tabular model.

2. In-context learning replaces training. RPT is built for in-context learning on tables: given labeled rows of a table it has never seen, it predicts the missing values of new rows. My 64 context rows define the task at request time. Change the labels and you change the behavior on the very next move. There is no retraining, no new deployment, and no Tetris-specific model to maintain.

3. Only the ranking matters. The game doesn't need RPT to reproduce the heuristic score to the decimal. It only needs the best candidate to get the highest prediction. A systematic offset in the predictions does no harm as long as the order is right.

How well did it learn?

I ran RPT-1.6 (live, SAP AI Core, K = 64, compact columns) against its teacher and a random player (meaning placing every block randomly) on the same two seeds, 100 pieces each:

Player Seed 1 lines Seed 2 lines Survived 100 pieces
Random00no (died after 27 and 14 pieces)
El-Tetris heuristic (the teacher)3839yes
SAP RPT-1.63835yes

And per decision, comparing RPT's choice to what the teacher would have chosen:

Metric Seed 1 Seed 2
RPT picks the teacher's move91%81%
Teacher's move is in RPT's top 3100%96%
Rank correlation of all candidates (Spearman, mean per move)0.9870.988
Median latency per move1.44 s1.44 s

A rank correlation of 0.99 means RPT orders all 9–34 candidates of a move almost exactly like the formula it never saw. Where it differs, it usually picks a move the teacher rates nearly as high. In Figure 2, RPT picked "rotation 1, column 3" (no new holes), while the teacher preferred "rotation 0, column 7" (clears a line). Both are reasonable moves.

This result needs one qualification. In this setup RPT learns to imitate a teacher, so matching the teacher is the ceiling, not a surprise win. It is a plausibility test: the model recovers a decision rule purely from examples, in real time, without training. I did not show that RPT plays better Tetris than the heuristic.

Note: On the same game engine and with the same rules (one decision per piece, no fallback), I also tested three decision models: TypeSafe Jev and two open-weight models I deployed myself on SAP AI Core, Laya and GEV-26B. Unlike RPT, they decide zero-shot, without example rows (Unlike RPT, they get no example rows. Instead they receive a short written instruction describing a good move (clear lines, avoid new holes, keep the stack low and flat)).
All three answered faster than RPT-1.6 (about 0.3–0.6 s vs. 1.4 s per move) but played less accurately. Measured as lines cleared relative to the heuristic: RPT-1.6 95%, GEV-26B 93%, Jev 88%, Laya about 6%. These come from separate runs (RPT: 2 games × 100 pieces; the others: 3 games × 200 pieces), so read them as a rough ranking. RPT-1.6 large was the slowest of all. TabPFN-3.5 Plus was rate-limited throughout my runs, so I have no result for it.

Making it run in real time

In the live game the pieces keep falling while RPT thinks. One prediction takes about 1.4 s on my AI Core deployment, so the game uses two tricks:

  • Pipelining. As soon as RPT has decided piece N, I compute the board after that move and immediately ask about piece N+1. The next decision overlaps with the current piece falling.
  • Speculation. In parallel, I also ask about piece N+1 on the board the teacher's move would produce. RPT usually agrees with the teacher, so in the recording 83% of these speculative answers were usable straight away. That pushes the game to about one piece per second.

There is no fallback. If RPT's answer does not arrive before the piece locks, the piece falls uncontrolled, like a player who does not press a key. In the recorded game, RPT controlled 47 of 48 pieces; one fell uncontrolled because a single call exceeded my 4-second timeout. With higher levels in Teris, pieces fall faster which then ofcourse cross the threshold in which RPT can decide, causing it to fail eventually.

Cost stays small: a move is one request of about 1,800 cells. With the per-cell prices configured in my demo, a 100-piece game came to about €0.09.

Why this matters beyond Tetris

Tetris is a toy, but the pattern is not:

  1. List the options a decision has (placements, suppliers, routes, discount levels).
  2. Describe each option as a row, with features that describe its consequences.
  3. Put labeled examples in the context: past decisions and how they turned out, or the judgment of an expert rule.
  4. Let RPT predict an outcome per option and pick the best.

That loop needs no training pipeline and no ML model per use case, and changing the goal is a data change, not a deployment. Business data lives in tables anyway.

The obvious next step for my Tetris demo is to replace the teacher's labels with what actually happened: score each past move by the lines it led to and the holes it caused over the next few pieces. Then RPT would learn from experience instead of imitating a formula, and its ceiling would no longer be the teacher's. But that is a experiment for the next post 🙂

Setup: SAP RPT-1.6 (sap-rpt-1.6) on SAP AI Core, 64 context rows, 18 columns, one request per piece with up to 34 candidate rows. Game engine, server and UI: TypeScript. Measurements from live runs on 21 October 2026.

entry.title: SAP Ariba Source to Contract 2611 Release Key Innovations Preview
entry.content:
Hey SAP Community!

The 2611 release is right around the corner, and I wanted to give you a heads-up on some of the things our teams have been working on across Strategic Sourcing, Strategic Contracts, and Public Sector Sourcing.

Honestly? A lot of this release is about fixing friction. Not big flashy features — just the stuff that slows people down in their daily work. I think you'll recognize a few of these.

Let's walk through them.

 

SAP Ariba Strategic Sourcing

Ability to Edit Decimal Place Limits in Terms for All Items

You can finally update decimal place limits for multiple items at once instead of doing it one by one.

If you've ever set up a sourcing event with dozens of line items and had to configure each one individually, you already know why this matters. It's one of those changes that won't make headlines but will absolutely save your team time every single time you set up an event.

 

Enhancements to the Grading Comments Capability in Guided Sourcing

Grading comments in guided sourcing now support attachments. Both the Consensus grading page and the Grade as a team member page.

This came up a lot in customer conversations — teams were writing paragraphs in comments trying to describe a document or reference a scorecard, when really they just needed to attach a file. Now they can. It's a small addition but it makes the whole grading experience feel a lot more complete.

 

Sync Latest Supplier Qualification Status in Guided Sourcing Events

Picture this: you're deep into an evaluation and awarding process, and you find out a supplier's qualification status changed after you pulled them into the event. Your event is showing old data. What do you do?

Until now, there wasn't a great answer. With 2611, you can manually trigger a sync of qualification status from Supplier Management directly into the event. One action, and you're working with current data again. It sounds simple because it is — but it makes a real difference when you're trying to make confident award decisions.

 

Prevent Award Submission for Suppliers Not Configured in SAP Master Data Governance

For teams running SAP Master Data Governance, this one's about catching a problem before it becomes a problem. If a supplier isn't set up in MDG, the system will now block the award submission right then and there — rather than letting it go through and creating a mess downstream.

It's a guardrail, plain and simple. And if you've ever had to untangle an MDG-related data issue after an award already went through, you know exactly why this matters.

 

Ability to Add Article Master Items in Guided Sourcing

This one closes a gap that's been bothering a few of our customers for a while. If you needed to kick off master data creation for an item in a guided sourcing event, you had to leave the event to do it. That's disruptive, and it happens at a point in the process where you really don't want to be jumping between screens.

Starting with 2611, you can trigger that master data creation flow directly from the Items table — right there in the Monitor phase, without going anywhere else. And it works the same way no matter how the item got into the event. Consistent, in-context, done.

 

Ability to Reopen ETendering Events

Public sector procurement doesn't leave a lot of room for improvisation — which is how it should be. But sometimes something happens after an eTendering event closes that genuinely requires a do-over, and teams have needed a proper way to handle that.

Now event administrators can reopen an ET event as a defined exception procedure. It's controlled, it's auditable, and it gives public sector teams an official mechanism for situations that used to require awkward workarounds.

 

Running Bid History Reports in the Background for Large Supplier Responses

If you run high-volume sourcing events, you've been there — waiting on a bid history report to finish generating while 100+ supplier responses churn through the system. It's a lot of time to just sit there.

Starting in 2611, when an event has more than 100 supplier responses, the report runs in the background. You get notified when it's ready. Go do something else in the meantime. It's a practical fix for a real frustration, and I think teams running large-scale sourcing events are going to feel this one quickly.

 

SAP Ariba Contract Management

Quick Access to Supplier Engagement Details from Contract Workspaces

OK this one is genuinely one of my favorites in the release, and it's not complicated at all. When you're in a contract workspace and you need to check the related supplier engagement, the engagement request ID is now a link. Click it, you're there.

And when you're done on the engagement details page, there's a back link that takes you straight back to the contract workspace. That's it. It sounds almost too simple to call out, but if you regularly move between contracts and engagements, you've felt this pain. No more hunting.

---

As always, these feature updates will go live with the 2611 release. Once published, you can use the official feature IDs on help.sap.com for deeper technical documentation. Stay tuned for our additional upcoming blog posts and follow me to stay informed on upcoming feature releases across SAP Ariba. 

Thank you for being a part of the SAP Ariba community and we look forward to continuing our journey of innovation together!
